title: The Turn of the Screw
image: The Turn of the Screw main cover.png
author: Henry James
summary: A young governess takes charge of two orphaned children, Miles and Flora, at a country house called Bly, on condition that she never troubles their uncle in London. She begins to see a man and a woman about the grounds, and learns that the last valet and the last governess are both dead. Henry James published the story in 1898, and readers still disagree about whether the ghosts are there.

Chapter summaries and historical context
Key quotations and discussion of themes
Critical perspectives on the governess’s account

sections.heading: The story told at Bly
paragraphs: A young governess accepts employment at a country house called Bly. Her employer, the uncle of Miles and Flora, lives in London and requires her to manage the children without troubling him. At the house she works with Mrs Grose, the housekeeper. Miles returns from school after being expelled, but the reason for his dismissal is initially withheld.

The governess sees a man whom Mrs Grose identifies from her description as Peter Quint, a former servant who is now dead. She also reports seeing Miss Jessel, her predecessor. She becomes convinced that these figures are seeking access to the children. The account follows her attempts to watch, interpret and intervene, with the children’s safety increasingly bound up with her certainty about what she has seen.

sections.heading: The frame and the manuscript
paragraphs: Before the events at Bly begin, a group of guests exchange ghost stories at a Christmas gathering. Douglas promises to read a manuscript written by a woman he knew: the governess. A separate narrator reports the gathering and transmits her account. These layers of narration belong to James’s fiction and are part of the complete text.

The governess therefore speaks retrospectively, describing both events and her earlier thoughts about them. Mrs Grose supplies information about the household, but readers receive her responses through the governess’s record. Keeping these different kinds of evidence distinct is useful when following the plot: an event described by the narrator, a report from another character and a conclusion drawn from either need not carry the same weight.

sections.heading: First publication and later revision
paragraphs: The Turn of the Screw appeared in 1898, first as a serial in Collier’s Weekly and then in the volume The Two Magics, where it was paired with Covering End. Its publication in a periodical preceded its independent life as a frequently reprinted novella.

James returned to the story when preparing his collected New York Edition, published in 1908 for this volume. The later presentation includes an authorial preface and revisions. Those publication stages are useful reference points when comparing quotations across editions. The purchase link on this page identifies the Astor edition described here; publication history of James’s work is separate from the date of an individual modern printing.

sections.heading: Henry James and the governess’s position
paragraphs: Henry James was born in New York in 1843 and spent much of his adult life in Europe, settling in England. His fiction includes novels, novellas and short stories, often concerned with what people know about one another and how they acquire that knowledge. The Turn of the Screw gives those questions a particularly restricted setting: one house, a small household and a narrator charged with responsibility.

The governess has authority over the children while remaining an employee. Her employer’s prohibition on contacting him removes an obvious source of advice. Mrs Grose knows the household’s history, yet the two women occupy different positions within it. These arrangements are stated in the narrative and help explain how information is exchanged, withheld or interpreted at Bly.

sections.heading: Using the Astor supporting material
paragraphs: Chapter summaries provide a reference to the sequence of appearances, conversations and discoveries. Historical context supplies background to the household and the circumstances in which the novella was published. Key quotations give readers passages to examine in their surrounding scenes.

The critical perspectives support comparison of different accounts of the governess’s narrative. The page does not prescribe a single solution to every uncertainty. A useful approach is to follow the evidence in order, recording who sees an apparition, who identifies it and what is inferred about the children. That makes disagreement about the story precise and keeps it connected to James’s wording.

title: Julius Caesar
author: William Shakespeare
summary: Caesar comes home from his victory over Pompey’s sons, and Cassius works on Brutus until he agrees to join the conspiracy. They stab Caesar in the Capitol on the Ides of March. At the funeral Antony’s speech sets the crowd against them, and the conspirators end up dead at Philippi.
editionIncludes: Complete play
Scene recaps and contextual notes
Key quotations and themes
Critical commentary for reading and study

sections.heading: Conspiracy, assassination and civil war
paragraphs: Julius Caesar opens in Rome after Caesar’s victory over Pompey’s sons. Public celebration is interrupted by officials who challenge the crowd’s shifting loyalties. Cassius then approaches Brutus, seeking support for a conspiracy against Caesar. Brutus agrees to participate because he fears what Caesar might become if given still greater power.

The assassination takes place in the third act, leaving two acts to examine its consequences. Brutus allows Antony to address the funeral crowd after speaking himself. Antony’s speech changes the public response, and the action moves towards the opposing military camps of Brutus and Cassius, and Antony and Octavius. The battles at Philippi end the conspirators’ campaign.

sections.heading: The first printed text
paragraphs: Julius Caesar was first printed in the 1623 First Folio. No earlier quarto printing is known. The Folio is consequently the principal early printed witness behind subsequent editions, although modern editors make decisions about punctuation, spelling, stage directions and particular readings.

The play is usually dated to 1599 and associated with the early Globe theatre. The surviving record of a Roman tragedy seen by Thomas Platter in London that September is commonly connected with Julius Caesar. The date of first performance and the date of first printing should be kept distinct: the text reached print more than two decades after its probable first staging.

sections.heading: Plutarch and Roman history
paragraphs: Shakespeare drew on Thomas North’s English translation of Plutarch’s Lives, published in 1579, particularly the lives of Caesar, Brutus and Antony. The source supplied incidents, character descriptions and speeches that the play reshaped for performance. Plutarch himself wrote long after the late Roman Republic, so neither source nor play is a contemporary record of Caesar’s death.

The historical assassination took place on the Ides of March, 44 BCE. The play condenses events and brings political argument into encounters between a relatively small number of speakers. Its dramatic chronology allows the public funeral, personal quarrels and military decisions to follow one another closely. Reading it beside its sources helps identify what Shakespeare selects and rearranges.

sections.heading: Speeches and the public audience
paragraphs: Brutus explains his action to the citizens in prose, asking them to assess his motives and his concern for Rome. Antony speaks after him, working within the permission he has been given while drawing attention to Caesar’s wounds, his will and the conspirators. The crowd’s responses are written into the scene, so the speeches can be studied as exchanges with an audience.

The citizens are also present at the beginning of the play and in the killing of Cinna the poet. That episode makes a mistaken identification a matter of life and death: the poet’s name is confused with a conspirator’s. It gives a concrete consequence to the disorder that follows the funeral, beyond the claims made by either political leader.

sections.heading: Private scenes and supporting characters
paragraphs: Portia questions Brutus about his changed behaviour and asks to share knowledge of his affairs. Calpurnia urges Caesar to remain at home after a disturbing dream. In each case a private conversation precedes a public decision, and the reasons offered within the household are later challenged or displaced.

The quarrel between Brutus and Cassius places their alliance under pressure after the assassination. They dispute money, accusations of corruption and military policy. These scenes provide evidence for comparing the principles characters announce with the decisions they make under practical strain. The commentary and selected quotations in the Astor edition support that comparison scene by scene.

sections.heading: Reading this edition
paragraphs: The scene recaps keep the sequence of events clear, while the contextual material explains Roman names, institutions and circumstances relevant to the action. Key quotations and the discussion of themes are starting points for close reading.

For study, it is useful to distinguish Caesar the historical figure, the Caesar presented by other characters and the man who appears on stage. Similar care is needed with Brutus: Cassius’s recruitment, Brutus’s private reasoning and Antony’s later account represent different perspectives within the play. The Astor supporting material allows those perspectives to be compared against the text.

title: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court
image: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court Main Cover.png
author: Mark Twain
summary: Hank Morgan, head superintendent at the Colt arms factory in Hartford, is knocked out in a fight and wakes up near Camelot in the year 528. He saves himself from the stake by predicting an eclipse, then starts building telegraph lines, newspapers and factories. Twain’s novel appeared in 1889, and this edition follows the first-edition text.
editionIncludes: Complete 1889 first-edition text, including the framing narrative and final postscript
Chapter summaries and researched context
Original American spelling, dialect and newspaper misspellings retained
Twain’s two authorial footnotes distinguished from the editorial note
Publication history, character studies, critical perspectives and glossary

sections.heading: The novel and its narrative
paragraphs: After a blow to the head in a Connecticut factory, Hank Morgan finds himself in sixth-century Britain. His knowledge of an approaching eclipse gives him authority at Arthur’s court, where he becomes known as the Boss. He introduces schools, newspapers, telephones, factories and new weapons, while travelling among the people whose society he proposes to reorganise.

Twain presents Hank’s account through a framing encounter and a manuscript. This edition includes the Preface, ‘A Word of Explanation’, ‘The Stranger’s History’, ‘The Tale of the Lost Land’, all forty-four numbered chapters, and the concluding manuscript material and final postscript. The frame is part of the novel as James wrote it.

sections.heading: The 1889 publication
paragraphs: Charles L. Webster & Company published the American edition in December 1889. Chatto & Windus issued the British edition that month under the different title A Yankee at the Court of King Arthur. The American title page used A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, although the cover used a shorter form.

The original American volume included illustrations by Daniel Carter Beard. The Astor editorial material discusses those illustrations and their place in the book’s publication history. This edition does not reproduce Beard’s original illustrations.

sections.heading: The text in this edition
paragraphs: The novel follows the complete 1889 first-edition text. Twain’s American spellings, inconsistent hyphenation and deliberate misspellings remain, including the typographical mistakes in the Camelot Weekly Hosannah. The text is not rewritten into modern English.

Changes concern presentation: the scene break in Chapter XV becomes a printed ornament, and the borrowed Malory chapter, newspaper passages and proclamations are displayed separately. Twain’s own footnotes in Chapters XIX and XXII appear with asterisks. A single editorial footnote in Chapter XVI uses a dagger. The textual note explains these distinctions so readers can identify what belongs to Twain and what the edition supplies.

sections.heading: Twain, printing and machinery
paragraphs: Samuel Langhorne Clemens, who wrote as Mark Twain, was born in Missouri in 1835. He worked as a printer, Mississippi river pilot and newspaper writer before establishing his career as an author. His earlier books included The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Life on the Mississippi and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.

Printing and invention also occupied him outside literature. He was involved in the publishing firm Charles L. Webster & Company and invested heavily in the Paige typesetting machine. The edition places this practical involvement with industrial technology alongside Hank’s career as a factory foreman, without treating the fictional narrator as a straightforward statement of Twain’s own opinions.

sections.heading: Arthurian sources and historical context
paragraphs: The supporting material identifies the Arthurian literature on which Twain drew, including Thomas Malory, and distinguishes borrowed passages from Hank’s narration. It also examines the nineteenth-century revival of interest in Camelot, which provides a different context from the remote period in which Hank’s adventures take place.

Historical sections address monarchy, inherited rank, slavery, work and political economy. These subjects occur in concrete episodes: Hank and the king travel in disguise, encounter poverty and disease, and are themselves sold as slaves. The later chapters bring industrial weapons into conflict with the institutions Hank has tried to replace.

sections.heading: Commentary and reference material
paragraphs: Chapter summaries are accompanied by researched context, allowing a reader to review events and then investigate particular historical references. The introductory material includes a chronology, an account of the narrative framework, language and style, character studies, and a separate discussion of the book’s argument.

Critical perspectives and reception history record how the novel has been read, while the glossary and bibliography provide reference points for further study. The edition’s purpose is to keep the complete novel available alongside information about its sources, publication and historical vocabulary, with authorial and editorial material clearly identified.

title: A Doll’s House
author: Henrik Ibsen
summary: Years ago Nora Helmer forged her dead father’s signature to borrow the money that saved her husband’s life. Now Krogstad, the man who lent it, is about to lose his job at Torvald’s bank, and he still has the forged paper. Ibsen’s play was first performed in Copenhagen in 1879; Astor uses R. Farquharson Sharp’s translation of 1910.
editionIncludes: Complete play in R. Farquharson Sharp’s 1910 translation
Line numbering throughout all three acts
On-page explanatory footnotes and notes on Ibsen’s original wording and figures
Act-end summaries and contextual material
Norwegian law, Laura Kieler, publication, performance and critical history

sections.heading: The Helmer household
paragraphs: The play takes place over three Christmas days in a Norwegian household. Torvald Helmer’s new appointment at a bank appears to promise greater financial security for his wife Nora and their children. Nora, however, has concealed a loan she obtained years earlier to finance a journey undertaken for Torvald’s health.

The lender, Krogstad, threatens to expose the forged signature used to secure that loan. Mrs Linde, an old friend seeking work, and Doctor Rank, a regular visitor, also enter the household. Ibsen confines the action to the Helmers’ rooms, where conversations, visits and the arrival of letters progressively reveal the circumstances behind the family’s apparent prosperity.

sections.heading: Publication and first performance
paragraphs: Et dukkehjem was published on 4 December 1879. Its first printing comprised 8,000 copies. The premiere followed at the Royal Theatre in Copenhagen on 21 December, with Betty Hennings playing Nora. The edition treats the printed play and its production history together, giving readers the chronology of its first appearance before following later performances.

The first public British production took place at London’s Novelty Theatre on 7 June 1889, with Janet Achurch as Nora and Charles Charrington as Helmer, using William Archer’s translation. That production belongs to the play’s reception history; the English text printed in this Astor edition is Sharp’s later translation.

sections.heading: The English translation and numbering
paragraphs: This edition uses R. Farquharson Sharp’s English translation, published by J. M. Dent in Everyman’s Library in 1910. Sharp is credited as translator and Haydn Wood as editor. The translation is identified explicitly because Ibsen’s play circulates in several English versions with differences of vocabulary, phrasing and theatrical emphasis.

The prose is numbered by printed line throughout all three acts. These numbers belong to this edition’s layout and provide a means of referring to particular passages. Explanatory notes appear on the page, with attention to places where Sharp anglicises Ibsen’s Norwegian monetary figures or wording. The notes supply the original information alongside the translated text.

sections.heading: Norwegian law, money and marriage
paragraphs: The historical material explains the legal and financial circumstances relevant to Nora’s borrowing. It describes the restrictions on married women in Norway at the time of the play, and the reforms that came later.

The commentary also addresses money, employment and household arrangements. These details matter to the action: Torvald’s bank position, Krogstad’s concern about his employment, Mrs Linde’s need for work and Nora’s private repayments all have specific financial circumstances. Act-end context panels accompany the summaries, connecting such references to the scenes in which they occur.

sections.heading: Laura Kieler and the alternative ending
paragraphs: A section on the writer Laura Kieler examines the documented parallels between her circumstances and Nora’s story. It preserves an important qualification: Kieler later denied committing forgery and sought a public clarification from Ibsen. Her life is therefore not presented as an exact factual version of the play.

The edition also explains the alternative ending Ibsen supplied for German performance. In a letter of February 1880 he explains that he disliked the change, and made it himself so that no one else would rewrite the play. This material helps distinguish the original conclusion from a historically documented adaptation of it.

sections.heading: Reading and performing the play
paragraphs: The supporting matter covers Ibsen’s background, the play’s publication, theatrical staging, critical responses and screen history. The notes on Doctor Rank explain the play’s medical language and what it suggested at the time, but they do not name a disease that Ibsen leaves unnamed.

For readers, the summaries establish the sequence of events across the three acts. For students and performers, numbered lines and on-page notes provide practical reference points for close examination of speeches, pauses and exchanges. The historical chapters keep the play’s Norwegian circumstances and the later decisions of translators and theatre practitioners visible as separate parts of its history.

title: American Christmas Stories
author: Various authors
summary: ‘A Visit from St. Nicholas’, usually credited to Clement Clarke Moore, appeared without a name in the Troy Sentinel in December 1823 and gave Santa Claus eight named reindeer. It is collected here with eight complete American Christmas stories written between 1872 and 1905, from Bret Harte to O. Henry, and six chapters of history.
editionIncludes: Eight complete stories plus ‘A Visit from St. Nicholas’
Six original chapters on American Christmas history
Individual publication histories and identified copy-texts
Researched context boxes, chronology and glossary
Historical spelling, punctuation and dialect retained

sections.heading: The nine literary texts
paragraphs: The eight stories are Bret Harte’s ‘How Santa Claus Came to Simpson’s Bar’; Kate Douglas Wiggin’s The Birds’ Christmas Carol; William Dean Howells’s ‘Christmas Every Day’; Willa Cather’s ‘The Burglar’s Christmas’; Paul Laurence Dunbar’s ‘One Christmas at Shiloh’; L. Frank Baum’s ‘A Kidnapped Santa Claus’; Owen Wister’s A Journey in Search of Christmas; and O. Henry’s ‘The Gift of the Magi’.

The volume also prints ‘A Visit from St. Nicholas’, attributed to Clement Clarke Moore. Its first appearance in 1823 supplies the collection’s opening date; the stories extend from Harte’s 1872 tale to O. Henry’s 1905 story. All nine literary texts are printed complete.

sections.heading: How the volume is arranged
paragraphs: Part I, ‘The American Christmas’, consists of six historical chapters: ‘A Holiday by Statute’, ‘The Poem That Made Santa Claus’, ‘Nast Draws Him’, ‘The Week Between’, ‘The Christmas Number’, and ‘The Kettle and the Counter’. They examine legislation, verse and images of Santa Claus, plantation holidays, periodical publishing, charity and commerce.

Part II presents the eight stories, each introduced by a headnote identifying its first publication, the text used in this edition and relevant later history. Part III follows the material into film and theatre and examines familiar Christmas customs that developed after the period covered by the anthology.

sections.heading: Christmas as a historical subject
paragraphs: The opening chapters distinguish different stages in the holiday’s legal recognition. The edition discusses Louisiana’s 1837 legislation, the 1870 federal holiday provision for the District of Columbia and its later extension to federal employees elsewhere. They were separate steps; there is no single date on which Christmas became a national holiday.

Other sections trace how publishers, illustrators, shops and charitable organisations contributed to public observance. The chapter on the Christmas and New Year interval in the slave South uses historical evidence to examine who received a holiday and under what conditions. The chronology gives readers a dated framework for these developments alongside the literary publications.

sections.heading: Writers, places and publishing
paragraphs: The selection ranges from a California mining settlement to New York domestic life, with additional settings and social circumstances supplied by the other stories. Its authors wrote for different outlets and purposes. Wiggin’s novella was connected with fundraising for a free kindergarten; Howells’s story appeared in a children’s periodical; Cather published her Christmas story while working in Pittsburgh.

The headnotes give the publishing history of each story, and show how different their first readers were. Newspaper supplements, magazines and separately published books reached different readers. Their histories also explain why publication dates, copyright dates and the dates on book title pages sometimes need to be recorded separately.

sections.heading: Complete texts and editorial checking
paragraphs: Each story is printed from an identified copy-text, with its spelling, punctuation and dialect retained. The introductory note records two particularly consequential source checks. An abridged version of Harte’s story circulating online removes its opening third; the source was replaced to restore the complete story.

Several digital versions of ‘The Gift of the Magi’ contain damaged ligatures and an incorrect amount of change. The edition uses a text checked against the original, without those scanning errors. Historical language is left in the primary texts, with relevant explanation in the headnotes. The editorial apparatus distinguishes an author’s original wording from the context supplied for present-day readers.

sections.heading: Context and reference apparatus
paragraphs: Stone-coloured panels headed ‘Context’ provide historical facts tied to the material just read, including laws, prices, addresses and magazine issues. Seven chapters include an ‘Anachronism watch’ item that identifies which objects or customs belong to which period. There are no plot-summary boxes; the historical material takes their place.

A Christmas glossary, chronology, sources and further reading support the main chapters. The closing sections on stage, screen and later customs extend the account beyond first publication while keeping the anthology’s literary range clear: eight stories and one poem from 1823 to 1905, accompanied by original historical reporting and textual documentation.

title: American Ghost Stories
author: F. Marion Crawford, Ambrose Bierce, Ellen Glasgow and others
summary: Ten American ghost stories from 1878 to 1925, seven of them by women, among them Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, Ellen Glasgow and Edith Wharton. Nearly all first appeared in magazines, and the essays go back to the magazines, editors and publishers who printed them.
editionIncludes: Ten complete stories, 1878–1925
Six parts of original historical and literary essays
Named copy-texts with original spelling and punctuation
Context boxes, chronology, glossary and documented sources

sections.heading: The ten complete stories
paragraphs: The contents are The Upper Berth by F. Marion Crawford; The Middle Toe of the Right Foot by Ambrose Bierce; The Shadowy Third by Ellen Glasgow; The House That Was Not by Elia Wilkinson Peattie; An Itinerant House by Emma Frances Dawson; The Shadows on the Wall by Mary E. Wilkins Freeman; The House of the Nightmare by Edward Lucas White; Bewitched by Edith Wharton; The Little Room by Madeline Yale Wynne; and The Shell of Sense by Olivia Howard Dunbar.

The earliest first appearance represented is Dawson’s An Itinerant House in 1878; the latest is Wharton’s Bewitched in 1925. The settings include a ship’s cabin, a hospital and private sickroom, farms, roads and houses whose occupants disagree about what is present. Each of the ten stories is reproduced in full.

sections.heading: The texts used
paragraphs: Each story is headed by information identifying its source edition. Eight are taken from collections assembled by their authors or publishers. Bierce’s The Middle Toe of the Right Foot and Dunbar’s The Shell of Sense are taken from Dorothy Scarborough’s Famous Modern Ghost Stories, published in 1921.

Spelling and punctuation follow the named copy-texts. Where the historical evidence disagrees about a date or a detail of someone’s life, the notes say so. The stated first-publication range describes the histories of the stories; it does not mean that every text has been transcribed from its first magazine appearance.

sections.heading: Six parts of editorial material
paragraphs: The Inheritance introduces the American ghost story’s literary and historical background. The Magazine Ghost examines payment, periodical publication, Christmas annuals and illustration. Houses That Do Not Stay Put discusses stories in which the house or room itself is in question.

Away From Home considers encounters at sea and on the road. The People Who Were Paid To Be There examines characters present because of employment, including a hired nurse and people accommodating paying visitors. Afterwards follows criticism, anthology selection and reprinting. These six parts precede the complete story texts and give the volume a researched subject beyond the selection alone.

sections.heading: Ghost stories as magazine publications
paragraphs: The essays place the stories in the commercial circumstances of their publication. Glasgow’s correspondence with her agent supplies evidence about the market for The Shadowy Third. Freeman’s supernatural stories appeared in Everybody’s Magazine before being collected, while Wharton’s Bewitched reached readers through Pictorial Review.

The volume also examines the relation between an annual’s cover date and the time it actually went on sale, using the publication of Crawford’s The Upper Berth in The Broken Shaft, a Christmas annual dated 1886. Such details help distinguish a printed date from evidence about circulation. Illustration is discussed as part of original publication history.

sections.heading: Dunbar, Scarborough and the later record
paragraphs: In 1905 Olivia Howard Dunbar argued in The Dial that the ghost had declined in American magazine fiction. Her own The Shell of Sense appeared in Harper’s Magazine in December 1908. Both the argument and the later story are discussed, giving the collection a documented example of a critic who also wrote supernatural fiction.

Dorothy Scarborough’s research and anthology work provide another part of the later record. The volume examines how stories were selected, grouped and made available to new readers. It also follows later critical work on Wynne and Peattie, distinguishing a published comparison between their stories from an unsupported assumption about influence.

sections.heading: Context boxes and reference material
paragraphs: The editorial chapters close with context boxes containing checkable details tied to the discussion. Where a chapter discusses a work not reproduced in this volume, a Story So Far section supplies its plot. For works reproduced in full, that summary section is omitted. Some boxes include an Anachronism watch note where a date affects what could have been present.

A chronology records publication and historical events, while the glossary defines words that occur in the ten stories and identifies the relevant story. Sources and further reading document the research on Spiritualism, psychical inquiry, magazine culture, domestic spaces and the later circulation of American ghost fiction.

title: The Blue Castle
author: L. M. Montgomery
summary: Valancy Stirling is twenty-nine, unmarried and ordered about by her family in the Ontario town of Deerwood. Then a doctor’s letter tells her she has a year to live, and she stops doing what she is told. Unusually for L. M. Montgomery, the novel is set in Ontario, not Prince Edward Island. It came out in 1926.
editionIncludes: Complete novel retaining Canadian spelling and punctuation
Explanatory footnotes and chapter summaries
Historical context on Muskoka, medicine, marriage, prohibition and motoring
Montgomery biography, manuscript history and publication research

sections.heading: Valancy Stirling and Deerwood
paragraphs: At twenty-nine, Valancy Stirling lives under the close supervision of her family in the fictional Ontario town of Deerwood. Her private refuge is the Blue Castle of her imagination. A medical consultation and the diagnosis that follows lead her to abandon habits of deference that her relatives have treated as permanent.

She goes to nurse Cissy Gay, whose circumstances have made her an object of local disapproval, and forms a relationship with Barney Snaith. Her choices take her beyond the familiar routines of the Stirling family. The narrative connects this change with work, companionship, illness and a different experience of the surrounding country.

sections.heading: A novel set in Ontario
paragraphs: The Blue Castle was published in 1926 by McClelland & Stewart in Toronto and the Frederick A. Stokes Company in New York. It is set in the Muskoka region of Ontario, where Montgomery and her family had holidayed in 1922. The local landscape and its recreational use provide a specific setting for the novel’s lake, island and woodland scenes.

The book has a different geographical setting from the Prince Edward Island world associated with Anne of Green Gables. Reading it within Montgomery’s career therefore brings attention to her adult life in Ontario as well as to the island of her childhood. The historical material in this edition supplies that biographical and regional background.

sections.heading: The text and manuscript history
paragraphs: The Astor edition retains Montgomery’s Canadian spelling and punctuation and adds explanatory material around the novel. The chapter summaries provide a reference to events, while footnotes clarify particular language and references. Historical context appears alongside broader discussion of the work’s composition, publication and reception.

The editorial material considers the manuscript as evidence of revision. Montgomery’s developing names and details can be compared with those in the published novel. The later publication of a manuscript edition, edited by Carolyn Strom Collins in 2024, has made that process more accessible. The Astor novel remains the published work described here, with manuscript history supplied as context.

sections.heading: Medicine, marriage and social expectation
paragraphs: Valancy’s diagnosis changes what she believes she can risk. So the doctor’s advice is part of the plot. The edition provides period information to help readers distinguish the fictional consultation from present-day assumptions about diagnosis and treatment.

The family’s response to Valancy’s conduct involves expectations about marriage, respectability and women’s behaviour. Her move into a household that her relatives disapprove of has practical social consequences. The notes explain relevant customs and circumstances without replacing the characters’ particular disagreements with a general account of every Canadian family in the period.

sections.heading: Objects, travel and the natural world
paragraphs: Motoring, patent medicines, household products and outdoor recreation belong to the material world of the novel. Identifying them can clarify a joke, an expense or a character’s habits. The historical sections also address prohibition and the treatment of alcohol, a subject connected with the reputations of people Valancy meets.

Descriptions of nature appear both directly and through the books of John Foster, the author Valancy admires. The text distinguishes her reading from her later experience of the island and woods. The supporting material on Muskoka gives geographical context for those passages, while leaving readers able to compare the fictional places with the documented region.

sections.heading: Montgomery and this edition
paragraphs: Lucy Maud Montgomery was born in 1874 on Prince Edward Island. The success of Anne of Green Gables in 1908 established a career that continued through novels, short stories and poetry. Her journals and correspondence, alongside surviving manuscripts, provide substantial evidence for her working life.

This edition brings together biography, composition and publication history with chapter-level assistance. Its scope includes the people, places, laws and objects mentioned in the novel, as well as critical perspectives on its reception. Readers can use the summaries to relocate an episode, consult a footnote for a particular reference, or read the longer essays alongside the complete text.

title: Carnacki, the Ghost-Finder
image: Carnacki, The Ghost Finder Main Cover.png
author: William Hope Hodgson
summary: Carnacki, a Chelsea bachelor with a camera and an ‘electric pentacle’, invites four friends to dinner and then tells them about his latest case. William Hope Hodgson published six of these stories in magazines in 1910 and 1912, and this edition prints them in that order, from the magazine texts.
editionIncludes: Six original stories, in magazine publication order
Magazine text distinguished from the reordered 1913 collection
Story summaries, explanatory footnotes and contextual panels
Documented textual emendations and restoration of British spelling
Essays on psychical research, apparatus, invented vocabulary and later stories

sections.heading: Six original cases
paragraphs: The stories appear in this order: ‘The Gateway of the Monster’, ‘The House Among the Laurels’, ‘The Whistling Room’, ‘The Horse of the Invisible’, ‘The Searcher of the End House’, and ‘The Thing Invisible’. Five were published in The Idler in 1910; the sixth appeared in The New Magazine in January 1912.

These are the six Carnacki stories published during William Hope Hodgson’s lifetime. Three further stories were collected posthumously in the expanded 1947 volume. The Astor edition discusses those later additions in its editorial matter, but its primary-text selection is the original six-story sequence. It is not advertised as the later nine-story collection.

sections.heading: Carnacki and his investigations
paragraphs: Thomas Carnacki investigates reported hauntings and then describes his cases to four friends gathered at his home in Cheyne Walk, Chelsea. His equipment includes a plate camera, sealing wax, microphones, a revolver and the Electric Pentacle. Practical tests of a building’s physical conditions accompany his use of occult texts and protective rituals.

The cases do not all reach the same kind of conclusion. Some involve human deception; others retain supernatural or unresolved elements. The introductory section ‘Six Cases, Six Verdicts’ examines those differences, while material on the Cheyne Walk frame explains how the investigations are presented as recollections told to a recurring group of listeners.

sections.heading: Magazine order and the 1913 book
paragraphs: Eveleigh Nash collected the six stories in London in March 1913. That book put ‘The Thing Invisible’ first, changing the order in which magazine readers had encountered Carnacki. This edition instead begins with ‘The Gateway of the Monster’ and ends with ‘The Thing Invisible’, restoring the sequence of first publication.

The source text also preserves readings associated with the magazine printings. The textual note records examples, including the butler’s name in ‘The Gateway of the Monster’ and a sentence added to the collected version of ‘The House Among the Laurels’. Readers comparing this volume with an edition descended from the Nash book will therefore find deliberate textual differences.

sections.heading: Textual decisions and notes
paragraphs: The copy-text is the Project Gutenberg transcription of the magazine versions. Two emendations are documented: ‘gallows-iron’ replaces an inconsistent ‘galley-iron’, and the name Garder is restored where the same authority is otherwise called Carder. British spellings are restored from a list printed in the edition; other American forms are left alone.

Irish dialect spellings and defensible period usages remain. Other doubtful readings are left as printed and discussed in the notes. Paragraphing, scene breaks and italics follow the copy-text. The stories have no authorial footnotes: the footnotes in this volume are editorial, and each story’s original magazine number is given with its title.

sections.heading: Hodgson and psychical research
paragraphs: Hodgson was born in 1877 and spent years at sea before working as a physical-culture instructor and writer. Photography was one of his practical interests. His earlier novels included The Boats of the ‘Glen Carrig’, The House on the Borderland and The Ghost Pirates; the Carnacki series followed in the magazine market.

The supporting essays place the stories beside the activities of the Society for Psychical Research, founded in 1882, and earlier fictional investigators such as Le Fanu’s Hesselius, Flaxman Low and Blackwood’s John Silence. Separate sections examine Carnacki’s apparatus and Hodgson’s invented terminology, keeping fictional occult authorities distinct from actual organisations and technologies.

sections.heading: The reading apparatus
paragraphs: A summary and contextual panel follows each story. The notes explain historical references, unusual vocabulary and practical details of the investigations. The introductory material covers Hodgson’s life, a chronology, the making and reception of the stories and their later history.

A glossary and bibliography support further reading. The emphasis is on making the original magazine series understandable on its own terms: how the cases were ordered, which version of the text is printed, what equipment existed at the time, and where Hodgson’s invented procedures depart from the period’s documented attempts to investigate supernatural claims.

title: Selected Poems of Samuel Taylor Coleridge
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
summary: Forty-three poems, as Arthur Symons chose them for his selection of 1905 and in the text James Dykes Campbell established. In the Ancient Mariner, the prose gloss Coleridge added in 1817 is back in the margin beside the verse, where he put it.
editionIncludes: 43 poems, including the major narratives, conversation poems, lyrics and satires
Text based on Campbell’s 1893 edition through Arthur Symons’s 1905 selection
Line numbers at intervals of five and explanatory footnotes
The Ancient Mariner’s 1817 gloss printed alongside the relevant stanzas
Publication history, chronology, contextual essays, critical perspectives and glossary

sections.heading: The selection
paragraphs: The volume includes ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’, both parts of ‘Christabel’, ‘Kubla Khan’, ‘Dejection: An Ode’, ‘Frost at Midnight’, ‘The Eolian Harp’ and ‘This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison’. It extends beyond these frequently anthologised works to political verse, short lyrics, satires and poems written or published late in Coleridge’s life.

Seven poems open the selection’s initial narrative and ballad group, from the Mariner to ‘The Three Graves’. Later contents include ‘France: An Ode’, ‘Fears in Solitude’, ‘Youth and Age’, ‘Work Without Hope’, ‘The Pains of Sleep’, ‘Limbo’ and the concluding ‘Epitaph’. The forty-three poems are a selection from Coleridge’s work.

sections.heading: The source text
paragraphs: The poems follow Arthur Symons’s Poems of Coleridge, published by Methuen in 1905. Symons drew on the text established by James Dykes Campbell for the Poetical Works of 1893. The Astor edition identifies this transmission explicitly and follows the selection’s order while adding its own editorial apparatus.

Spelling, punctuation and capitals are left as they were printed. The textual note records corrections to demonstrable transcription faults, including misread dates and verse lines broken by the electronic source’s fixed line length. It also distinguishes such corrections from the edition’s decisions about the presentation of glosses, footnotes and line numbers.

sections.heading: The Ancient Mariner and its gloss
paragraphs: Coleridge first published the Mariner in Lyrical Ballads in 1798 and revised it for later appearances. The marginal prose gloss was added in Sibylline Leaves in 1817. Symons transferred that gloss to an appendix; this edition returns it to an outer column opposite the stanzas it describes.

Coleridge’s own footnote acknowledging Wordsworth in Part IV is also printed at the foot of its page. These are authorial elements, distinct from the explanatory notes supplied by the Astor editor. Their placement allows the verse, Coleridge’s later commentary and the new annotations to be consulted together without confusing their authorship.

sections.heading: Numbering and explanatory apparatus
paragraphs: Line numbers appear at intervals of five and continue across the parts of an individual poem. They count the lines as printed in this edition. The textual note explains that differences from another edition’s numbering may arise from lineation, especially in irregular poems, and should not automatically be read as missing text.

Editorial footnotes are numbered afresh for each poem. Historical and contextual material accompanies the poetry, supported by a glossary and bibliography. The jointly written ‘The Devil’s Thoughts’ is identified as a work by Coleridge and Robert Southey; its inclusion does not make Southey the author of the other forty-two poems.

sections.heading: Coleridge’s life and literary circle
paragraphs: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was born at Ottery St Mary in 1772. His association with William and Dorothy Wordsworth in Somerset was central to the period in which he wrote the Mariner, the first part of ‘Christabel’ and several of the conversation poems. Lyrical Ballads appeared anonymously in 1798.

The edition’s biographical and contextual chapters also cover Southey, Charles Lamb, Coleridge’s journalism, his political interests and his later life at Highgate. A separate medical-history discussion addresses opium through the historical record. These chapters provide circumstances for reading individual poems without reducing every work to an episode in the poet’s biography.

sections.heading: Where the poems first appeared
paragraphs: The publication history follows the poems through collected books, pamphlets, newspapers and gift annuals. Important volumes include Poems on Various Subjects in 1796, Lyrical Ballads, the 1816 publication of Christabel with ‘Kubla Khan’ and ‘The Pains of Sleep’, and Sibylline Leaves in 1817.

Nine poems in the selection first appeared in daily newspapers. A dedicated section records that aspect of Coleridge’s work, alongside chronology, sources and influences, language and style, critical perspectives and reception history. The resulting apparatus connects particular poems to their first audiences and subsequent textual history, while preserving the selected poems themselves in full.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest
image: Importance of Being Ernest Main Cover.png
author: Oscar Wilde
summary: Jack Worthing is Ernest in town and Jack in the country; his friend Algernon has invented an invalid called Bunbury so that he can get out of dinners. Both are in love with women who say they could only marry a man called Ernest. Wilde’s play opened at the St James’s Theatre on 14 February 1895, and this edition follows the first book edition of 1899.
editionIncludes: Complete three-act 1899 first book text, corrected by Wilde
Explanatory footnotes
Act summaries and historical context
Composition, publication and performance history
Character studies and critical perspectives

sections.heading: Jack, Algernon and their invented identities
paragraphs: Jack Worthing uses the name Ernest when visiting London and has explained his absences from the country by inventing a troublesome brother. Algernon Moncrieff has invented an invalid friend, Bunbury, whose illnesses supply convenient reasons to avoid social obligations. Their arrangements become difficult to maintain when Algernon visits Jack’s country house as the supposed brother.

Gwendolen Fairfax and Cecily Cardew each believe that the name Ernest has a particular importance for the man they intend to marry. Lady Bracknell investigates Jack’s suitability as a husband, while Miss Prism and Dr Chasuble become involved in plans for christenings and the discovery of Jack’s origins. The action moves from a London flat to a country garden and drawing room.

sections.heading: The 1899 text used here
paragraphs: The edition follows the first book text published in 1899, the three-act version corrected by Wilde for publication. This textual basis is significant because the play survives in several forms. An earlier four-act version and the text used in the original 1895 production are distinct stages in its history.

The notes explain how the versions differ. The printed play retains Wilde’s subtitle, A Trivial Comedy for Serious People. Explanatory footnotes identify language and references in the chosen text, while act summaries provide a convenient record of the developing misunderstandings.

sections.heading: First performance and publication
paragraphs: The Importance of Being Earnest opened at the St James’s Theatre in London on 14 February 1895. George Alexander managed the theatre and played Jack Worthing. The comedy’s production belongs to the final months of Wilde’s public success before the trials and imprisonment that interrupted his theatrical career.

The first book edition followed in February 1899, issued by Leonard Smithers. Its title page named the author only as ‘the author of Lady Windermere’s Fan’. The recorded issue comprised 1,000 numbered ordinary copies, 100 signed large-paper copies and twelve signed Japanese-vellum presentation copies. These figures describe the first edition, not the Astor paperback.

sections.heading: What the footnotes explain
paragraphs: Wilde’s jokes frequently depend on contemporary social practices: visiting and dining, country houses, family connections, education, inheritance and the investigation of a prospective marriage. The notes explain the places, institutions, customs and terms that a first audience could have recognised more readily than a reader today.

The distinction between a practical obstacle and a verbal joke is often important. Jack’s uncertain parentage affects Lady Bracknell’s judgement of him; the proposed christenings concern the names preferred by Gwendolen and Cecily. Notes supply context for these actions while keeping the complete dialogue available for readers to judge the characters’ stated reasons.

sections.heading: Letters, diaries and family evidence
paragraphs: Cecily’s diary gives an already elaborate history to a relationship that has scarcely begun. Gwendolen’s record and Cecily’s account then help produce the confrontation in the garden. Written evidence appears authoritative to its keeper even when its contents reflect wishes or inventions.

The final act turns on a different set of documents and recollections. Miss Prism’s earlier employment, the lost manuscript and the hand-bag found at Victoria Station connect Jack’s history with the family before him. The comedy’s explanations depend on specific objects and testimony. Character studies in the Astor material follow these roles through the three acts.

sections.heading: Wilde and the supporting essays
paragraphs: Oscar Wilde was born in Dublin in 1854 and studied at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford. His published work includes poetry, fiction, criticism and plays. The London society comedies brought his work to a substantial theatrical audience in the 1890s.

The Astor introduction places Earnest within that career and documents its composition, revision, first production and later reception. Critical perspectives accompany the text without requiring the reader to accept a single account of its humour or social argument. The combination of the identified 1899 text, footnotes and act summaries makes the edition suitable for sustained reading as well as reference to individual scenes.

title: M. R. James: Collected Ghost Stories
image: M.R. James Ghost Stories Main Cover.png
author: M. R. James
summary: M. R. James, Provost of King’s College, Cambridge, and later of Eton, wrote many of his ghost stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas. All thirty-three that he finished are here, from the four original volumes, the 1931 collection and three later stories, with seven pieces James wrote about the ghost story itself.
editionIncludes: 33 completed ghost stories
Story summaries and researched context
Publication histories and first-appearance details
Seven writings by James on ghost-story composition
Biography, chronology, glossary and essays on sources and afterlives

sections.heading: The extent of the collection
paragraphs: The volume gathers thirty-three completed ghost stories. Twenty-six come from James’s four original collections: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary, More Ghost Stories, A Thin Ghost and Others, and A Warning to the Curious and Other Ghost Stories. Four further completed stories were added to the collected edition of 1931.

The remaining three are The Experiment, The Malice of Inanimate Objects and A Vignette, published after the 1931 collection. The Astor contents therefore extend beyond a simple reprint of that collected volume. The distinction is useful when comparing editions described as collected or complete, because their actual contents can differ.

sections.heading: From separate volumes to collected stories
paragraphs: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary appeared in 1904, followed by More Ghost Stories in 1911, A Thin Ghost and Others in 1919, and A Warning to the Curious and Other Ghost Stories in 1925. The collections include such stories as Canon Alberic’s Scrap-book, The Mezzotint, Count Magnus, Casting the Runes and Oh, Whistle, and I’ll Come to You, My Lad.

The publication histories give the date each story first appeared, which is often years before the collection. Some stories were read to friends before publication; others appeared in periodicals or small separate printings. Those settings help explain how James’s fiction reached its first audiences.

sections.heading: James’s academic life and his fiction
paragraphs: Montague Rhodes James was born in 1862 and died in 1936. He was a scholar of medieval manuscripts and apocryphal literature, and served as Provost of King’s College, Cambridge, and later of Eton College. His scholarly work included the description and cataloguing of manuscript collections.

The fiction repeatedly involves readers, collectors and people investigating old buildings or objects. A manuscript, print, inscription, whistle or archaeological discovery can initiate a story. The Astor biographical and historical material explains James’s working knowledge of such things, while distinguishing documentary sources from claims that a particular event directly caused a fictional episode.

sections.heading: The text and the explanatory material
paragraphs: The edition preserves James’s spelling, punctuation and foreign-language forms. Story summaries provide a record of what happens, and researched context explains details that can otherwise be difficult to place. The glossary and chronology offer further reference points alongside the individual stories.

The supporting essays discuss antiquarian sources, actual locations, illustrations, Christmas readings and the history of reception. Discussion of illustrations in an original collection should be understood as publication history; the edition features listed here describe the Astor text and apparatus. Where a geographical identification or source connection is uncertain, it should remain distinguishable from a documented fact.

sections.heading: James on writing ghost stories
paragraphs: Seven pieces by James on the ghost story are included alongside the fiction. They allow readers to consult his own statements about the form and its composition. Such writing gives a different kind of evidence from later critical accounts: it records what James chose to say about the stories, their methods and the conditions of telling them.

The essays can be read beside individual tales without making every fictional detail an illustration of a fixed rule. James’s narrators differ in their access to events, and stories may be transmitted through conversations, documents or reports. The edition gives readers the fiction and the author’s commentary together so those differences can be examined directly.

sections.heading: Reception and adaptations
paragraphs: James’s stories have continued to circulate through anthologies, readings, radio and screen adaptations. Casting the Runes supplied the source for Jacques Tourneur’s 1957 film Night of the Demon. Television versions have also helped bring particular stories to audiences who first encounter them outside the printed collections.

The Astor material records publication and adaptation history while keeping the original stories central. Readers can use it to locate the source of an adaptation, identify the collection in which a story first appeared, or place a late story within James’s career. The retailer link identifies this thirty-three-story edition; availability is determined by the retailer for the reader’s location.

title: The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson
author: Mark Twain
summary: Roxy, enslaved and one-sixteenth Black, swaps her baby son with her master’s baby in the cradle, so that her child will grow up free and white. Years later, in the Missouri river town of Dawson’s Landing, a murder trial is settled by the fingerprints David Wilson has been collecting as a hobby. This edition follows the 1894 American text and lists its corrections.
editionIncludes: Complete novel based on the 1894 American edition
Twain’s language, punctuation and dialect retained
Chapter summaries and explanatory notes
Context on Missouri slavery, race, inheritance law and fingerprinting
Chronology, publication history, critical record and glossary

sections.heading: Dawson’s Landing and the exchanged children
paragraphs: The novel begins in Dawson’s Landing, a fictional Missouri town on the Mississippi. Roxy, an enslaved woman, secretly exchanges her infant son with her master’s child. The boys grow up occupying one another’s legally assigned positions, while the town continues to treat their supposed ancestry as a reliable basis for identity and status.

David Wilson, a lawyer whose misunderstood joke earns him the name Pudd’nhead, collects fingerprints as a private interest. More than twenty years after the exchange, a murder brings his collection into court. The edition supplies chapter summaries to clarify the sequence of discoveries without substituting a shortened retelling for Twain’s narrative.

sections.heading: Serial and book publication
paragraphs: Pudd’nhead Wilson appeared in seven instalments of The Century Magazine from December 1893 to June 1894. Chatto & Windus published the first British book edition in 1894. The American Publishing Company of Hartford issued the first American edition on 28 November that year, using the longer title The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson and the Comedy Those Extraordinary Twins.

The American volume appended Those Extraordinary Twins, the comedy separated from the developing novel during composition. That companion work belongs to the publication history discussed here; this Astor volume presents the complete Pudd’nhead Wilson novel. Its contents comprise ‘A Whisper to the Reader’, twenty-one chapters and the conclusion.

sections.heading: Which text is printed
paragraphs: The copy-text follows the first American edition of 1894 through its Project Gutenberg transcription. A small number of readings are corrected against the Harper & Brothers edition of 1899. These interventions are documented, while Twain’s spelling, punctuation and dialect otherwise remain as printed.

The edition closes the spaces the original compositors inserted into contractions and resolves hyphens created solely by line breaks. It does not generally modernise the prose. The distinction matters particularly where a spelling belongs to dialect or a speaker’s individual language. Notes on the text and a separate textual introduction explain the relationship between the original setting and this edition.

sections.heading: Slavery, law and identification
paragraphs: Historical chapters examine slavery in Missouri, the legal classification of ancestry, inheritance and the threat of sale farther south. These subjects explain the consequences attached to the children’s exchange within the novel’s society. Dawson’s Landing is also considered as a river town with institutions and social practices connected to Twain’s experience of Missouri.

A separate section discusses fingerprints and identification. The edition places Wilson’s unusual collecting habit and its use at the trial alongside the developing history of identification methods. The novel’s events and the real history of fingerprinting are dated separately, so readers can follow both.

sections.heading: Twain and the novel’s composition
paragraphs: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in 1835 and grew up in Hannibal, Missouri. Before becoming established as Mark Twain, he worked in printing, piloted Mississippi steamboats and wrote for newspapers. His experience of a slaveholding river community supplies relevant background to a novel whose early chapters are set before the Civil War.

The composition history examines the transformation of material about twins into the published novel. Twain drafted the work while living in Italy in the early 1890s. The edition also places it within his later career, including the financial difficulties surrounding his publishing business, while distinguishing those biographical circumstances from the experiences of individual fictional characters.

sections.heading: Editorial and critical material
paragraphs: The front matter includes a short life of Twain, publication details, chronology, composition and sources, an introduction and an account of the narrative framework. Sections on language and dialect and on Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar give separate attention to the characters’ speech and the aphorisms printed with the chapters.

Contemporary reception, stage and screen history, and the later critical record document the book’s reception over time. A glossary, explanatory notes and bibliography provide reference material alongside the chapter apparatus. Readers can therefore consult the legal, historical and textual information relevant to a passage without losing the distinction between Twain’s original novel and the new commentary.

title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
image: Rime of the Ancient Mariner hardcover.png
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
paperbackImage: Rime of the Ancient Mariner Main Cover.png
deck: An old sailor, a wedding guest and a dead albatross: Coleridge’s poem of 1798.
editorial: The 1834 text with the 1817 marginal gloss and continuous line numbers.

sections.heading: The poem in successive editions
paragraphs: The first printed title was ‘The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere’. Its deliberately old-fashioned spelling helped present the poem as a ballad from an earlier period. In the 1800 Lyrical Ballads, much of that spelling changed and the title became ‘The Ancient Mariner’. The poem also moved from the opening of the 1798 collection to a position near the end of the first volume, immediately before ‘Tintern Abbey’.

The material before the poem changed as well. Early versions supplied an ‘Argument’ outlining the voyage. In 1817 Coleridge replaced that introduction with a Latin epigraph from Thomas Burnet concerning unseen beings and the limits of human knowledge. The 1834 text printed by Astor belongs to the end of this process of revision. Its 625 numbered verse lines remain separate from the accompanying 1817 gloss and the edition’s new commentary.

The verse uses the alternating longer and shorter lines associated with the ballad, but the stanza length varies. Four-line stanzas occur beside expanded forms, and repetition appears within as well as between lines. Continuous numbering makes those variations easier to cite without counting the prose gloss as part of the verse.

sections.heading: Wordsworth’s recorded response
paragraphs: Wordsworth appended a notably mixed assessment to the poem in the 1800 edition of Lyrical Ballads. He said that Coleridge had wished to suppress it, while explaining his own reasons for retaining it. His objections concerned the Mariner’s limited individual character, his lack of agency, the connection between events and the accumulation of imagery.

The same note praised the poem’s feeling, its presentation of emotion and its verse. Wordsworth praised the variety achieved in the verse even while judging the metre unsuitable for a long poem. This response is useful evidence of the poem’s earliest reception within the collaboration itself: admiration and disagreement were present before the later marginal gloss, collected editions and subsequent critical reputation.

sections.heading: The Somerset collaboration
paragraphs: Coleridge moved to Nether Stowey in Somerset in 1796. William and Dorothy Wordsworth lived nearby at Alfoxden during the particularly productive period of 1797–1798. The Mariner belongs to the same period as ‘Frost at Midnight’, ‘Fears in Solitude’, ‘The Nightingale’ and the first part of ‘Christabel’.

Lyrical Ballads was published anonymously in 1798, combining work by Coleridge and Wordsworth. Their contributions did not use one uniform kind of narrator or subject: the supernatural voyage appeared beside poems about ordinary encounters, recollection and rural life. Coleridge later discussed their literary conversations in Biographia Literaria. He wrote that account nearly twenty years after the events, and the edition treats it as a memoir.

title: Edgar Allan Poe: Selected Tales
image: Selected Tales- Edgar Allan Poe Main Cover.png
author: Edgar Allan Poe
summary: Poe revised his stories again and again, so every edition has to choose a version. This one prints ten tales, among them ‘The Fall of the House of Usher’, ‘The Tell-Tale Heart’, ‘The Black Cat’ and two of the Dupin detective stories, and says for each which printing it follows.
editionIncludes: Ten complete tales, first published between 1839 and 1849
Story summaries and researched historical context
Publication histories for every tale
A textual note identifying revised versions and significant textual choices
Original material on Poe, magazine publishing, Gothic fiction and early detective stories

sections.heading: The ten tales
paragraphs: The contents are The Tell-Tale Heart; The Black Cat; The Cask of Amontillado; The Fall of the House of Usher; The Oval Portrait; The Masque of the Red Death; The Pit and the Pendulum; Hop-Frog; The Murders in the Rue Morgue; and The Purloined Letter. Each story is printed complete. The selection is Astor’s; Poe never published a collection under this title.

The selection includes accounts of murder and concealment, an artist’s fatal absorption in a portrait, Prince Prospero’s attempt to exclude plague, a prisoner’s efforts to understand his confinement, and the revenge of a court entertainer. The two Dupin stories bring a different kind of narrative: an unnamed companion records investigations that distinguish an explanation of the evidence from the assumptions made by the police.

sections.heading: Publication in magazines and gift-books
paragraphs: These ten tales first appeared between 1839 and 1849 in magazines, newspapers and annual gift-books. The Pit and the Pendulum and The Purloined Letter, for example, first appeared in The Gift, an annual, and not in a collection of Poe’s. The edition records the original publication setting of each story.

Poe worked as a magazine editor and reviewer as well as a writer. Stories were revised, reprinted and moved between periodicals and books during his lifetime. The supporting material explains that publishing environment and follows particular transactions, including the appearance of The Tell-Tale Heart in the first number of James Russell Lowell’s The Pioneer in 1843, for which Poe received ten dollars.

sections.heading: Which versions are printed
paragraphs: The textual note preserves distinctions between first publication and the version selected for this edition. The Purloined Letter follows Tales of 1845, while acknowledging later manuscript alterations in Poe’s copy owned by J. Lorimer Graham. Those later changes are not silently substituted for the chosen printed text.

The Oval Portrait and The Masque of the Red Death use Poe’s revised forms. The earlier version of The Oval Portrait was titled Life in Death and included an opening subsequently removed. By stating these choices, the edition allows readers to understand why a familiar story can differ from its earliest magazine appearance without treating every reprint as an identical text.

sections.heading: Narrators and investigations
paragraphs: Several stories give the account of events to someone directly implicated in them. The Tell-Tale Heart begins with a defence of the speaker’s sanity; The Black Cat offers a condemned man’s explanation; The Cask of Amontillado recounts a calculated act of revenge. What their narrators claim can be checked against what they say they did.

In the Dupin stories, the narrator instead watches another person analyse a problem. The Murders in the Rue Morgue concerns apparently impossible violence in a Paris room, while The Purloined Letter concerns a stolen document and an unsuccessful official search. These stories are important early examples of detective fiction; the edition places them in the history of investigation without implying that their procedures describe actual police practice.

sections.heading: Historical references and Poe’s reputation
paragraphs: The contextual material supplies information about magazine culture, Gothic conventions and the historical references behind the tales. It distinguishes the story-world of The Pit and the Pendulum from the documented history of the Spanish Inquisition. Readers can therefore recognise an invented setting or device without assuming that every incident in the fiction has a direct historical equivalent.

Biographical material also examines the evidence behind Poe’s reputation. Accounts associated with Rufus Wilmot Griswold, whose hostile portrayal helped shape later ideas about the author, require checking against letters and other records. The edition weighs those sources as historical documents and does not use the more sensational stories about Poe to explain his fiction.

sections.heading: Using the edition
paragraphs: Story summaries provide a record of events, while the historical sections explain references and circumstances surrounding publication. These are separate tasks: a summary establishes what happens, and a contextual account identifies information outside the story. The complete tales remain available for close reading alongside that supporting material.

Readers interested in the supernatural can compare Usher, the portrait and Prospero’s sealed rooms; readers interested in narration can compare the three accounts of criminal acts; and readers approaching detective fiction can read the Dupin stories together. The contents list and textual note make clear that this is ten stories, not Poe’s complete fiction.

title: Seven Pillars of Wisdom
image: Seven Pillars of Widsom Main Cover.png
author: T. E. Lawrence
summary: T. E. Lawrence lost most of the first draft of this book at Reading station in 1919 and rewrote it from memory. Astor prints the 1926 text he had privately printed for about two hundred subscribers, and separates his own account of the Arab Revolt from what the documents record.
editionIncludes: Complete 1926 Subscribers’ text as issued for general circulation in 1935
Summaries and context after each of the twelve major divisions
Lawrence’s preface, dedicatory poem, headnotes, epilogue and back matter
Explanatory notes, chronology, glossary and publication history
Historical discussion of the Arab Revolt, military strategy and Lawrence’s account

sections.heading: Lawrence’s account of the Arab Revolt
paragraphs: Seven Pillars of Wisdom records Lawrence’s part in the Arab Revolt of 1916–1918. The narrative follows his association with Emir Feisal and campaigns involving Akaba, the Hejaz Railway and Damascus. It combines descriptions of journeys and military operations with recollections of individuals, political discussions and arguments about irregular warfare.

The historical apparatus treats it as a personal account written and revised after the events. Lawrence’s descriptions and figures are retained, including passages that differ from military records. Where the memoir disagrees with later evidence, the commentary points it out and the memoir is left as Lawrence wrote it.

sections.heading: The 1926 Subscribers’ text
paragraphs: This edition follows the text prepared for the 1926 Subscribers’ Edition, as issued for general circulation by Jonathan Cape in 1935. It is therefore distinct from the longer 1922 Oxford text and from Revolt in the Desert, Lawrence’s shorter abridgement published in 1927.

The copy-text is the Standard Ebooks transcription, derived from Colin Choat’s Project Gutenberg of Australia text and checked against digital scans. Lawrence’s punctuation, paragraphing and inconsistent spellings of Arabic names remain. The textual note explains that those inconsistencies were deliberate preferences Lawrence defended when his proofreader proposed standardising them.

sections.heading: What is included in the volume
paragraphs: The complete subscribers’ text includes Lawrence’s preface, the dedicatory poem, eleven book headnotes, the epilogue and his own back matter. Four authorial footnotes are marked with symbols, while the numbered notes elsewhere are editorial. The Greek expressions occurring in the narrative are supplied in transliteration.

The chapter removed before the 1926 printing and restored by Cape from 1940 is not included as part of the subscribers’ text; its history is explained in the editorial material. The original plates and folding maps are not reproduced. Lawrence’s account of commissioning the illustrations and his list of them remain in the back matter.

sections.heading: The book’s publication history
paragraphs: Lawrence’s account passed through several substantially different manuscripts and printings. The edition traces the lost 1919 draft, subsequent rewriting, the privately printed Oxford text of 1922 and the revision produced for subscribers in 1926. It explains why references to a ‘complete’ Seven Pillars need to specify which version is meant.

The expensive production of the subscribers’ volume led to the further abridgement published as Revolt in the Desert in 1927. Seven Pillars itself reached a general reading public after Lawrence’s death in 1935. The history of these versions is presented separately from the wartime chronology, so the dates of composition and revision are not confused with the dates of the campaign.

sections.heading: Lawrence before and after the campaign
paragraphs: Thomas Edward Lawrence was born in 1888. He studied history at Oxford, investigated Crusader castles and worked on archaeological projects in the Middle East before the First World War. He served in wartime intelligence in Cairo before travelling to the Hejaz in 1916 and becoming attached to Feisal.

The biographical material follows his involvement in postwar diplomacy and later service in the Royal Air Force and Tank Corps under assumed names. It also places his writing, translation work and technical interests within that later career. Lawrence died in 1935, shortly before the subscribers’ text was issued for general circulation.

sections.heading: Historical and reading apparatus
paragraphs: Summaries headed ‘The Story So Far’ and researched ‘Context’ material follow the twelve major divisions. The notes work book by book, with no box after each chapter. It gives readers a way to review the campaign’s changing locations, participants and objectives across a long narrative.

The introductory and reference material covers the Arab Revolt, First World War politics, military strategy, the Hejaz Railway, people and places, and the critical reception of Lawrence’s account. A chronology, glossary, explanatory notes and publication history provide practical support for reading the text while keeping its particular version and its limits as historical testimony clear.

title: The Awakening
author: Kate Chopin
summary: Edna Pontellier, twenty-eight, married to a New Orleans businessman and the mother of two boys, spends a summer at Grand Isle and learns to swim. By the autumn she has moved out of her husband’s house. Reviewers in 1899 disliked the book so much that Kate Chopin published very little afterwards. It is printed here in the first-edition text, without footnotes.
