sections.heading: Edna Pontellier and the course of the novel
paragraphs: Edna Pontellier, her husband Léonce and their children spend the summer at Grand Isle, off the Louisiana coast. There Edna forms a close attachment to Robert Lebrun and begins to question the domestic arrangements of her married life. Swimming, conversation, painting and music have particular places in that summer, and each returns in the later narrative.

Back in New Orleans, Edna gives up her Tuesday at-homes and the other social duties Léonce expects of her. She pursues painting, moves into a smaller house and conducts relationships on terms that differ from the life expected of her. Chopin follows these decisions through Edna’s encounters with Robert, Alcée Arobin, Adèle Ratignolle and the pianist Mademoiselle Reisz. The final chapter returns to Grand Isle.

sections.heading: Composition and first publication
paragraphs: Chopin began the novel in 1897 and completed it on 21 January 1898. Its original title was A Solitary Soul. Herbert S. Stone & Company published The Awakening in Chicago on 22 April 1899. These dates distinguish composition from publication.

The Astor text follows the first edition of 1899. It prints the whole novel. Publication history accompanies the text, allowing readers to place the novel beside Chopin’s earlier writing and the contemporary publishing circumstances in which it appeared.

sections.heading: The Louisiana setting
paragraphs: Grand Isle, Chênière Caminada and New Orleans are identifiable places, and the edition treats them as such. The coastal resort and the city household offer different social settings; journeys between them are part of the novel’s construction. Historical material explains the resort culture, local geography and the hurricane of 1893, which devastated the coastal communities before Chopin wrote the novel.

The discussion of Creole society distinguishes that particular historical setting from Edna’s own Kentucky background. Material on marriage and property provides information about the legal and economic arrangements surrounding the Pontellier household. The account also attends to servants and racial divisions, so that the household’s relative leisure is not described as though it existed independently of other people’s work.

sections.heading: Music, work and domestic expectations
paragraphs: Edna’s painting and her encounters with music are specific activities in the narrative. Mademoiselle Reisz performs for listeners whose responses differ, while Adèle’s music belongs to another domestic setting. The supporting material identifies these episodes and their historical references, giving readers information with which to examine them directly.

The novel also repeatedly records money, visiting, childcare and the organisation of a home. Edna’s proposed independence therefore has practical as well as personal consequences. Contextual sections on marriage, property and social convention explain the conditions under which she acts; they do not replace the narrative with a single approved account of her decisions.

sections.heading: Chopin and the record of reception
paragraphs: Kate Chopin was born in St Louis in 1850 and spent important years of her married life in Louisiana. Her fiction includes both novels and short stories. The biographical and literary material situates The Awakening within that career, including its regional settings and the writers whose work she read.

The reception history distinguishes documented hostility from later repetition. No evidence has been found for the often-repeated claim that St Louis libraries banned the novel; the removal by Evanston Public Library in 1902 is a separate documented event. Similarly, the cancellation of the projected collection A Vocation and a Voice is recorded without inventing a reason for the publisher’s decision.

sections.heading: The Astor commentary
paragraphs: Chapter summaries and contextual material are placed at chapter ends, with no new footnotes introduced into Chopin’s narrative. Readers can consult the summaries to check the sequence of events and then turn to material on Louisiana life, music, race, language and literary influences. The layout preserves a distinction between the novel and its modern apparatus.

The critical sections describe how different scholars have read the novel, and do not present any one reading as fact. Alongside the publication and textual histories, these sections make it possible to study both the 1899 book and the later discussion that changed its standing. The edition describes the historical evidence behind its claims and keeps that evidence distinct from the characters’ words and the narrator’s account.

title: The Chimes
author: Charles Dickens
deck: Dickens’s second Christmas book, written in Genoa in 1844.

sections.heading: The surviving manuscript and first readings
paragraphs: The manuscript of The Chimes survives in the Forster Collection at the Victoria and Albert Museum. John Forster, Dickens’s friend and later biographer, inherited manuscripts and other working material; his library and collections reached the museum through his 1876 bequest. The manuscript places the story within a substantial surviving record of Dickens’s composition, proof correction and publication.

Dickens’s letters from Genoa refer to the bells heard during his stay there in 1844. Before publication he returned to London, corrected proofs and read the new work to groups of friends. Daniel Maclise recorded a reading in Forster’s rooms in a pencil drawing. Dickens’s letter to Catherine dated 2 December 1844 reports the powerful response of listeners to readings of the story, providing contemporary evidence of its effect before it reached the general public.

sections.heading: New Year, accounts and hospitality
paragraphs: The story’s full subtitle identifies bells ringing an old year out and a new one in. That calendar setting appears throughout the ordinary business surrounding Trotty’s vision. Shops display goods for the coming year, almanacs calculate its seasons, and Sir Joseph Bowley insists that every financial account should be settled before the year turns.

When Trotty admits owing money for rent and to Mrs Chickenstalker’s shop, Bowley treats the debt as evidence of personal failure. The detail is exact: Trotty owes Mrs Chickenstalker a small grocery bill. Later, Mrs Chickenstalker appears in the final gathering and proves to have a connection with Will Fern’s family. The same shopkeeper therefore belongs both to the world of everyday credit and to the hospitality with which the narrative ends.
The ending also gives the new date a practical consequence: the bells announce that Meg and Richard’s wedding day has arrived.

sections.heading: The story beyond its first readership
paragraphs: The Chimes circulated in forms beyond the ordinary reading copy. The Charles Dickens Museum holds a presentation copy given by Dickens to Hans Christian Andersen. It also preserves sheet music associated with the Christmas books, including ‘The Chimes Quadrille’. Such objects document the story’s movement through personal gifts, domestic music-making and the publishing trade.

The illustrations accompanying the original publication also form part of that history. Maclise’s frontispiece and his drawing of the private reading are different objects: one visualises the book’s supernatural subject, while the other records the author performing his manuscript for friends. These surviving documents help distinguish composition, first publication and later circulation. The Astor edition’s notes and contextual material discuss the literary work itself; the historical objects are evidence of how nineteenth-century readers and listeners encountered it.

title: The Diary of a Nobody
image: The Diary of Nobody Main Cover.png
author: George and Weedon Grossmith
summary: ‘Why should I not publish my diary?’ asks Charles Pooter, a City clerk who has just moved into The Laurels, Brickfield Terrace, Holloway. For fifteen months he records trouble with tradesmen, a humiliating ball at the Mansion House and his son Lupin’s schemes. It began as a series in Punch in 1888–89.

sections.heading: Charles Pooter’s diary
paragraphs: Charles Pooter, a City clerk, moves with his wife Carrie into the Laurels, a rented house in Holloway. He begins recording his daily life, arguing that an ordinary person has as much reason to keep a diary as a celebrated one. His entries describe household improvements, work, dinner invitations, friends and disagreements with his son, Lupin.

The sequence covers fifteen months of events, including visits from Gowing and Cummings, Lupin’s changing occupations and relationships, and Pooter’s attempts to maintain dignity during social mishaps. The book retains the diary form: what readers know comes through the details Pooter selects and the account he gives of his own conduct.

sections.heading: From Punch to the 1892 book
paragraphs: The Diary of a Nobody first appeared in twenty-six instalments in Punch between May 1888 and May 1889. J. W. Arrowsmith of Bristol published the expanded book in 1892. The book added roughly four further months of diary entries and included twenty-six illustrations by Weedon Grossmith.

The Astor editorial material follows the differences between serial and book publication and the novel’s later reception. The early book editions attracted limited attention; the 1910 issue, with prefatory tributes from Lord Rosebery and Augustine Birrell, helped establish a wider readership. Publication history is therefore part of the account of how the book acquired its later reputation.

sections.heading: The text and its presentation
paragraphs: This edition follows a public-domain transcription of an Arrowsmith book edition. It includes Mr Pooter’s introduction and the original chapter arguments, the short summaries printed beneath the chapter headings. The final chapter retains the source’s heading ‘Chapter the Last’, appearing as the twenty-fourth chapter in the contents.

The text has not been modernised. Historical spellings, punctuation and unusually frequent italics remain, as do Pooter’s misquotations, mistakes and mishearings. They are part of the book as printed and have not been corrected. The textual note distinguishes the original book’s contents from the summaries and explanatory material added for this edition.

sections.heading: The Grossmith brothers
paragraphs: George Grossmith and his younger brother Weedon both had careers in performance. George worked as an entertainer and became associated with leading comic roles in Gilbert and Sullivan’s operas. Weedon trained as an artist before developing a career as an actor, playwright and theatre manager.

Both brothers are credited as authors of the novel. The introductory biography connects their theatrical and professional backgrounds with the circumstances of the book’s writing and publication. Weedon Grossmith’s twenty-six drawings for the 1892 volume are discussed in the introduction but not reproduced; the ornaments in this edition are modern.

sections.heading: Holloway, work and domestic expenditure
paragraphs: The historical context examines Holloway as a London suburb and the City clerk as an occupation with particular expectations of respectability, dress and conduct. Pooter’s house, commuting, office relationships and social ambitions belong to this specific late nineteenth-century setting.

Money, furnishings, clothing, entertainment and domestic service recur in the diary. The notes explain period references and vocabulary so that an expense, invitation or household decision can be understood in its immediate circumstances. The commentary also attends to the difference between the position Pooter believes he holds and the responses he records from employers, tradespeople, friends and family.

sections.heading: Chapter apparatus and reference material
paragraphs: Each chapter is followed by editorial sections headed ‘The Story So Far’ and ‘Context’. These are additional to the Grossmiths’ original chapter arguments: one reviews what happens in the chapter, while the other supplies relevant historical information. Explanatory footnotes appear at the foot of the page.

The front matter includes biography, publication details, a textual note, chronology and material on the narrative framework, language and reception. A glossary provides reference support for unfamiliar expressions. Together these features allow the complete diary to be read alongside information about Victorian London, the authors’ careers and the novel’s changing readership, while leaving its original wording intact.

title: The Haunted Man and the Ghost’s Bargain
image: The Haunted Man and the Ghost's Bargain Hardcover.png
author: Charles Dickens
paperbackImage: The Haunted Man and the Ghost's Bargain Main Cover.png
deck: Dickens’s last Christmas book, from 1848: a chemist who asks to forget.
editorial: The complete story with chapter summaries and notes.

sections.heading: The publication’s family context
paragraphs: The Haunted Man appeared in the year Dickens lost his older sister Fanny, who died in September 1848. The Charles Dickens Museum records first-day sales of 18,000 copies. A surviving invitation from Catherine Dickens to Thomas Beard shows the family arranging a dinner at Devonshire Terrace on 3 January 1849 to celebrate the book’s success.

The invitation was written on mourning paper. It supplies a small but concrete document of the circumstances surrounding publication: a successful new Christmas book and a recent family bereavement belonged to the same household and the same season. That record provides biographical context for a story concerned with recollected suffering, without establishing that Redlaw’s experiences are a direct transcription of the author’s life.

sections.heading: The households affected by the bargain
paragraphs: Redlaw’s influence reaches people whose difficulties are already present before his intervention. The Tetterby household is crowded, short of money and occupied with the demands of children. Johnny’s responsibility for carrying the baby is a recurring detail of the family’s daily life. When Redlaw’s condition spreads, existing fatigue and dissatisfaction turn into hostility between people who had previously cared for one another.

The student known as Edmund also brings a separate family history into the story. His connection with the name Longford links his circumstances with people from Redlaw’s past. We learn of these connections through meetings and conversations. By the final meal in the old hall, the Swidgers, the student, the Tetterbys and the nameless child are all at the table, so Redlaw’s recovery is shared.
A remembered inscription beneath the portrait in the hall closes the narrative with an explicit appeal to preserve memory.

sections.heading: Dickens’s abandoned reading version
paragraphs: The Charles Dickens Museum preserves a copy of The Haunted Man that Dickens prepared for oral performance. He cut pages from the original 1848 edition, mounted them in a larger book and added highlighting and annotations. The resulting object records work on adapting the printed story to a spoken programme.

The museum dates its likely preparation to 1858, when Dickens began his first paid public-reading tour, and records that he abandoned the selection as unsuitable. A prepared reading copy should therefore not be mistaken for proof that he regularly performed the work. This abandoned version belongs beside the better-known theatrical afterlife of Pepper’s Ghost: one involved Dickens reshaping his prose for his own voice, while the other used a scene from the story in an optical stage demonstration. They are distinct episodes in the work’s performance history.

title: The House on the Borderland
image: The House on the Borderlands Main Cover.png
author: William Hope Hodgson
summary: Two Englishmen on a fishing holiday in the west of Ireland find a ruined house on the edge of a chasm and, in the rubble, a damaged manuscript. Its writer describes pig-faced creatures climbing out of the pit, and a vision in which he watches the sun die. William Hope Hodgson published the novel in 1908.

sections.heading: The discovered manuscript
paragraphs: Two friends, Tonnison and Berreggnog, on holiday in the west of Ireland, find the remains of a house and a damaged manuscript. Its unnamed writer, generally called the Recluse, describes his life in an isolated building with his sister and his dog, Pepper. The account includes attacks by swine-like creatures and investigations of a pit beneath the house.

The manuscript also describes experiences beyond the immediate siege: a vast plain, another house, changes in the apparent rate of time and visions of the solar system’s destruction. The framing travellers and the fictional editor are part of the presentation. The Recluse’s account reaches us incomplete, and nobody else confirms it.

sections.heading: First publication and composition
paragraphs: Chapman & Hall published The House on the Borderland in London in 1908. The first edition’s extended title described the manuscript as discovered in 1877 in ruins south of the fictional village of Kraighten. Hodgson’s Author’s Introduction carries the date 17 December 1907.

The edition examines surviving correspondence about the composition of Hodgson’s novels. Letters indicate that the manuscripts preceded their eventual publication by several years. It distinguishes the documentary evidence from the later identification of a manuscript called The House of Mysteries with The House on the Borderland, an attribution generally accepted but still dependent on inference.

sections.heading: The complete text
paragraphs: The text follows the Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1908 edition. The volume includes the Author’s Introduction, all twenty-seven numbered chapters, the intervening ‘Fragments’ and the closing poem ‘Grief’. No word of the novel has been added, removed or reordered.

Hodgson’s irregular punctuation, dashes, ellipses, capitalisation and spellings remain. Typographical repairs address broken spacing, quotation marks and the dateline of the introduction. Passages presented as doubtful or damaged manuscript material retain their original quotation marks. The textual note explains each of these decisions.

sections.heading: The fictional editor’s footnotes
paragraphs: The seventeen numbered notes in the source belong to the fictional editor who claims to prepare the manuscript for publication. They are part of Hodgson’s fiction, not explanatory footnotes newly written by Astor. Sixteen appear at the foot of the pages carrying their markers.

One source note has no surviving marker in the transcription used for this edition. Its wording is preserved in the textual note, and the numbering of the remaining notes is left unchanged. The edition does not invent a precise attachment point. This distinction keeps the original fictional apparatus separate from the new chapter summaries, context and introductory commentary.

sections.heading: Hodgson, Ireland and astronomy
paragraphs: William Hope Hodgson was born in Essex in 1877. His father’s work as an Anglican clergyman took the family to Ardrahan in County Galway during Hodgson’s childhood. Hodgson later spent years at sea, worked in physical culture and developed interests in photography before publishing novels and magazine fiction.

Two dedicated context essays examine the landscape around Ardrahan and the astronomy of the later chapters. The first considers the region’s geology and disappearing rivers; the second explains the scientific ideas relevant to the novel’s enormous timescales and celestial events. These provide documented contexts for the fiction without claiming that its supernatural experiences are scientific predictions.

sections.heading: Commentary and later reception
paragraphs: Chapter summaries review the narrative’s changing scenes and the relationship between the house, the underground spaces and the visionary passages. Historical context, character studies, key passages and an account of the narrative framework accompany the text. The glossary supports readers encountering unfamiliar terms or usages.

The reception history follows the novel beyond its original publication, including its reappearance in Arkham House’s 1946 collection of Hodgson’s four novels. Critical perspectives and afterlives address subsequent readings and adaptations. A chronology, sources and influences, and bibliography place this particular novel within Hodgson’s career and provide reference points for further study.

author: Stephen Crane
summary: In January 1897 Stephen Crane spent thirty hours in a dinghy off the Florida coast after the Commodore sank, and ‘The Open Boat’ is the story he made of it. The London edition of 1898 collected it with sixteen other stories in two parts, and Astor follows that order.

sections.heading: The seventeen-story collection
paragraphs: William Heinemann published The Open Boat and Other Stories in London in 1898. Its seventeen stories make it a different collection from the eight-story American volume, The Open Boat and Other Tales of Adventure. This Astor edition follows the fuller London contents and their original arrangement.

Part I, ‘Minor Conflicts’, contains eight stories, including the title story, Western and Mexican narratives and ‘Death and the Child’. Part II, ‘Midnight Sketches’, contains nine shorter pieces concerned largely with city life. The two headings are kept so that readers can see how the collection was organised.

sections.heading: Part I: Minor Conflicts
paragraphs: The first part contains ‘The Open Boat’, ‘A Man and Some Others’, ‘The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky’, ‘The Wise Men’, ‘The Five White Mice’, ‘Flanagan and His Short Filibustering Adventure’, ‘Horses’ and ‘Death and the Child’. The stories range across sea travel, gunfights, gambling, armed expeditions and wartime experience.

The title story draws on Crane’s survival of the wreck of the Commodore off Florida in January 1897. Four men occupy a small boat as they attempt to reach shore. The volume retains the London dedication to William Higgins, Captain Edward Murphy and steward C. B. Montgomery, connecting the published collection with the people involved in that experience.

sections.heading: Part II: Midnight Sketches
paragraphs: The second part comprises ‘An Experiment in Misery’, ‘The Men in the Storm’, ‘The Duel That Was Not Fought’, ‘An Ominous Baby’, ‘A Great Mistake’, ‘An Eloquence of Grief’, ‘The Auction’, ‘The Pace of Youth’ and ‘A Detail’. Several are brief studies of poverty, crowds, work or encounters in New York.

Their inclusion gives the book a wider range than a selection restricted to the shipwreck and Western stories. The editorial material considers how Crane’s reporting and observation supplied material for fiction, while the story apparatus identifies relevant circumstances of publication and setting for each individual piece.

sections.heading: The London copy-text
paragraphs: The copy-text is the Heinemann London edition of 1898. Its mixture of British and American spellings is left as it was. Section numerals also remain: six stories are divided into numbered sections, while eleven run without those internal numbers.

The textual note records differences between magazine and book versions. It also explains a correction to the contents listing: the first edition prints ‘Dual’ there, although the story’s own heading correctly reads ‘The Duel That Was Not Fought’. This edition follows the story heading. Centred rules replace two rows of asterisks used for additional breaks in the original setting.

sections.heading: Crane’s journalism and travels
paragraphs: Stephen Crane was born in Newark, New Jersey, in 1871. His writing developed through newspaper work, observation of New York’s poorer districts and fiction including Maggie: A Girl of the Streets and The Red Badge of Courage. The success of the latter brought him international attention while still in his twenties.

His travels included the American West and Mexico, the attempted voyage towards Cuba aboard the Commodore, and reporting on the Greco-Turkish War. He later worked as a correspondent during the Spanish-American War and lived in England. The edition connects these documented journeys with particular stories without assuming that every fictional incident directly reproduces a biographical event.

sections.heading: Sources, context and commentary
paragraphs: The introductory matter includes a biography, publication details, chronology, sources and influences, narrative framework and discussion of language and style. A section on filibustering in 1895–1898 explains the armed expeditions relevant to the Commodore voyage and other material in the collection. ‘Against the Record’ considers documentary evidence, while ‘In the Magazines’ follows the stories’ periodical appearances.

Story summaries, historical context and explanatory notes accompany the complete texts. Critical perspectives, reception history, glossary and bibliography provide additional reference material. The edition therefore identifies both the contents of this particular 1898 volume and the different reporting, magazine and book contexts from which its seventeen stories emerged.

title: The Railway Children
author: E. Nesbit
summary: When their father is taken away by two men one night, Roberta, Peter and Phyllis move with their mother to a cottage in the country beside a railway line, and start waving to the 9.15. Nobody tells them for a long time that he is in prison. E. Nesbit’s novel was serialised in 1905 and came out as a book in 1906.

sections.heading: The family at Three Chimneys
paragraphs: After their father is unexpectedly taken away, Roberta, Peter and Phyllis leave their comfortable London home with their mother. They settle at Three Chimneys, a country cottage near a railway, and learn to live with much less money. Their mother writes stories to support the family while keeping the circumstances of their father’s disappearance from them.

The children become acquainted with the station porter Perks and an elderly passenger whom they wave to as his train passes. Their adventures include a railway embankment collapse, a rescue in a tunnel and the arrival of a Russian exile. These events connect the family’s private difficulty with the work and journeys of the people around them, until the mystery of their father can be addressed.

sections.heading: From serial to book
paragraphs: The Railway Children was serialised in The London Magazine in thirteen instalments, from January 1905 to January 1906. Wells Gardner, Darton issued the book in 1906. The edition gives both first publications, the serial and the book.

The original book contained twenty black-and-white plates by C. E. Brock, including the frontispiece. Those illustrations belong to the history of the 1906 publication. This Astor edition discusses them but does not reproduce them; its additional material consists of historical and literary commentary around the complete text.

sections.heading: Railway work and travel
paragraphs: Nesbit’s railway is a place of employment as well as adventure. Perks’s responsibilities, the station routine, passing trains, signals and the need to stop an approaching engine give the story concrete practical circumstances. The children’s friendship with Perks the porter and the other railwaymen grows through many visits and small favours.

The contextual material explains Edwardian railways, the distinctions of class surrounding passenger travel and railway employment, and the technology and routines mentioned in the story. It also follows the children’s mistakes about what constitutes helping: Peter’s appropriation of coal and the attempted birthday gift to Perks both depend on differences between their intentions and another person’s understanding of the act.

sections.heading: Law, exile and the absent father
paragraphs: The father’s imprisonment and the Russian stranger’s history bring political and legal matters into a family narrative. The edition provides background on criminal justice, accusations of espionage and Russian exile, while preserving the order in which the children learn about these events. The historical material gives a basis for understanding references that the original audience could have recognised more readily.

The account also examines the Russo-Japanese War and the political atmosphere surrounding the novel’s first publication. These contexts are supplied as information about the period. They should not be confused with a claim that Nesbit’s plot is a direct transcript of one particular criminal case or that every incident has an identified real-life model.

sections.heading: Nesbit and the book’s later history
paragraphs: Edith Nesbit, who published as E. Nesbit, lived from 1858 to 1924. She wrote poetry and fiction for adults as well as the children’s books for which she became especially well known. The biographical material sets The Railway Children among Nesbit’s many other books.

The publication and adaptation sections trace the book’s subsequent life in print, on television, in film and in performance. They distinguish the details of Nesbit’s novel from choices made by later adapters. A reader who knows a filmed version can therefore use the complete text to establish which incidents, settings and speeches are present in the original book.

sections.heading: What the editorial material supplies
paragraphs: The novel has no footnotes added to it. Chapter summaries and contextual material accompany the story at chapter ends, while character studies and key-passage discussions appear in the supporting sections. A chronology, glossary and publication and textual histories provide reference material for readers who need to check names, dates and unfamiliar terms.

The historical accounts address railways, law, class and political events in relation to particular passages. The character material follows Bobbie, Peter, Phyllis, their parents and the people they meet, keeping their actions within the story’s sequence. Together these additions support reading the whole 1906 novel and identifying the historical circumstances behind it, while the text itself remains separate from the modern commentary.

sections.heading: Hester Prynne and the central story
paragraphs: The story opens in seventeenth-century Boston as Hester Prynne leaves prison carrying her infant daughter, Pearl. She must wear a scarlet letter A as a public punishment for adultery, but refuses to identify Pearl’s father. In the crowd she recognises her estranged husband, who subsequently adopts the name Roger Chillingworth and pursues the concealed father.

Hester supports herself through needlework and raises Pearl on the edge of the settlement. The minister Arthur Dimmesdale holds a position of public respect while carrying a secret that affects his health. Chillingworth gains access to him as a physician. The central action extends across seven years and culminates around Dimmesdale’s Election Sermon and a final public appearance on the scaffold.

sections.heading: The 1850 romance
paragraphs: Ticknor, Reed and Fields published The Scarlet Letter in Boston in 1850. Its subtitle identifies it as A Romance. That description is useful when approaching the book’s treatment of history: Hawthorne uses the Puritan past, but the work is not offered as a documentary reconstruction of a specific prosecution.

The narrative’s twenty-four chapters follow the longer introductory sketch The Custom-House. In that sketch, a narrator associated with Hawthorne’s own life describes discovering an embroidered letter and papers concerning its wearer. The claimed archival origin is part of the book’s fiction. Keeping this introduction with the main narrative preserves the way Hawthorne presents the relation between documents, memory and invention.

sections.heading: Hawthorne, Salem and historical inheritance
paragraphs: Hawthorne was born in Salem in 1804. His family history included John Hathorne, a judge involved in the Salem witch trials. His own employment at the Salem Custom House supplied material for the introductory sketch. These are different historical connections: one concerns inherited ancestry, the other the author’s direct experience of a nineteenth-century institution.

The edition sets those connections beside the seventeenth-century Boston of Hester’s story. Religious office, magistrates, public punishment and the supervision of family life belong to the world depicted in the romance. Historical information helps readers identify them without assuming that every judgement made by a fictional official states either an uncontested historical fact or Hawthorne’s own view.

sections.heading: The three scaffold scenes
paragraphs: The scaffold appears at three decisive points. Hester’s first appearance exposes her and Pearl while leaving Dimmesdale publicly protected by his position. The second takes place at night, when Dimmesdale joins Hester and Pearl in a scene unavailable to the daytime community. The final appearance returns them to public view.

The ending does not remove all disagreement. Witnesses offer different accounts of what they saw on Dimmesdale’s body, and some refuse the explanation accepted by others. The edition’s account of structure follows these three scenes closely, distinguishing the events narrated from the interpretations subsequently attached to them.

sections.heading: The letter and the four principal characters
paragraphs: The authorities impose the letter as a fixed sentence, but Hester has embroidered it before she leaves prison. Later neighbours associate the A with her abilities, while a light in the sky is given another explanation. These are particular readings made inside the narrative, and the close-reading material traces who makes them and under what circumstances.

The character studies treat Hester as a working mother as well as the object of punishment, Pearl as an observant child as well as a figure interpreted by adults, Dimmesdale as a minister living under concealment, and Chillingworth as a husband who chooses revenge. The character notes describe what each person does and how they relate to the others.

sections.heading: Reading the complete book with context
paragraphs: This Astor edition provides the complete text with chapter summaries, explanatory notes and supporting material on publication, form, history and reception. The Custom-House, the main narrative and the conclusion remain available in their sequence, allowing readers to follow the changes in evidence and public knowledge across the work.

The accompanying studies address narration, the scarlet letter, the scaffold scenes and the characters through precise episodes. Historical context and interpretation are distinguished: a date of publication can be documented, while an account of why Hester returns to Boston remains a reading to be tested against the text. Sources and further reading provide routes into Hawthorne’s historical setting and the continuing discussion of the romance.

title: The Wendigo
author: Algernon Blackwood
summary: A moose-hunting party goes into the backwoods north of Rat Portage, in Canada, and the guide, Défago, is called away in the night by something that shouts his name. Algernon Blackwood published the story in 1910. Astor’s text is set from the Project Gutenberg edition and has not been checked against the 1910 printing.
editionIncludes: Complete story, set from Project Gutenberg ebook 10897 presenting the 1910 text
Story summaries and researched contextual material
Canadian geography, hunting travel and Blackwood’s background
Documented discussion of windigo traditions and the Fiddler case
Publication, reception and adaptation history with the limits of the evidence stated

sections.heading: The hunting party
paragraphs: Five men travel into the Canadian wilderness in search of moose. Among them are Dr Cathcart, his nephew Simpson and the guide Joseph Défago. When the hunters separate into smaller parties, Simpson accompanies Défago into an area where the guide becomes increasingly disturbed by something beyond the visible camp.

During the night Défago disappears. The tracks that Simpson follows become difficult to explain, and the sounds and subsequent appearances reported by the party do not produce a settled account of what has happened. The complete tale follows the search and its aftermath, keeping the hunters’ differing reactions within a narrative of testimony, observation and fear.

sections.heading: First publication and the reading text
paragraphs: The Wendigo first appeared in The Lost Valley and Other Stories, published by Eveleigh Nash in 1910. The edition’s publication account identifies that collection as the first appearance and does not assert an earlier magazine publication. It also traces the story’s later reprinting and reputation as an individual work.

The Astor reading text is set from Project Gutenberg ebook 10897, first released in 2004 and presenting the 1910 story. A copy of the first edition has not been independently collated for this printing. The distinction is stated because the date of the original story and the identity of the electronic text used to typeset it are separate bibliographical facts.

sections.heading: Canada and Blackwood’s travels
paragraphs: The story’s country north of Rat Portage belongs to a real Canadian landscape. Material on geography, hunting, camps and movement through the bush supplies practical background to the expedition. Distances, unfamiliar terrain and dependence on a guide affect what the party can observe and how a search can be conducted.

The biographical material considers Blackwood’s Canadian experience and accounts of his travel. His biographer describes a hunting trip in 1898; the edition reports this as the biographer’s account and does not claim it as the source of the story. A link between his experience and the story is presented as possible, not proven.

sections.heading: Windigo traditions and the historical record
paragraphs: The supporting sections distinguish Blackwood’s fictional creature from windigo traditions in Indigenous communities. They give historical context and consider the ways in which such traditions were reported to non-Indigenous readers. A literary story published in London in 1910 is therefore not treated as an authoritative description of a single, uniform belief.

A separate account examines the Fiddler case in Canada, including the proceedings following the arrests of Jack Fiddler and Pesequan in 1907. Those events preceded publication of The Wendigo, but no direct connection between the case and Blackwood’s composition has been documented. Closeness in date is not treated as proof of influence.

sections.heading: Description, reception and adaptation
paragraphs: Blackwood does not supply a complete physical portrait of the creature. The story depends on what the men hear, on tracks and on the difficult evidence surrounding Défago. Later antlered or deer-skull images familiar from popular culture should therefore not be read back into the tale as though they were Blackwood’s own description.

The reception material follows the work into later discussion and adaptation. H. P. Lovecraft’s praise is given in relation to what he actually wrote, including his distinction between this story and The Willows. The edition does not convert a critic’s ranking into an invented quotation, or use an unprovable claim of uninterrupted publication as a substitute for a documented account of reprinting.

sections.heading: How the supporting material is arranged
paragraphs: Summaries record the development of the expedition and the events surrounding Défago’s disappearance. Contextual sections then address Blackwood, the Canadian bush, historical sources, windigo traditions and the story’s later reputation. This division allows readers to check the action before following a particular historical question into the supporting material.

The edition says what the evidence for each claim is. The electronic source of the reading text is identified; a first-edition collation is not claimed; a documented historical case is not declared the story’s source; and modern creature imagery is distinguished from the written account. These details make the volume useful for readers comparing supernatural fiction with the historical and geographical material from which later accounts of it have been constructed.

title: The Willows
author: Algernon Blackwood
summary: Two men canoeing down the Danube in flood tie up for the night on a sandy island among the willows below Pressburg, and cannot leave. Algernon Blackwood had made the same journey by canoe himself, a few years earlier. This is the original British text of 1907, printed without footnotes.
editionIncludes: Complete 1907 story in its original British text
Section summaries and factual contextual notes
Documentary material on Blackwood’s Danube voyage and the disputed date of the journey
Historical geography and the changing river landscape
Publication, textual and reception histories, with unfamiliar vocabulary explained

sections.heading: Two canoeists on the Danube
paragraphs: An unnamed narrator and his Swedish companion are travelling down the Danube when they camp on an island below Pressburg. The river is in flood. Sandbanks, channels and low willows surround a campsite exposed to the current and the wind, and the men must attend to ordinary practical matters such as shelter, food, fuel and the condition of their canoe.

The narrator begins to report sights and sounds that he cannot explain in the same terms. His companion’s apparent confidence gives way to a different account of the danger they face. The two men compare what they have noticed and try to decide whether they can leave, and no narrator steps in to explain what is happening.

sections.heading: The 1907 collection
paragraphs: The Willows first appeared as the third story in The Listener and Other Stories in 1907. In that volume it occupied pages 127–203. Its later publication as a separate story can obscure the fact that it originally formed part of a collection; the Astor publication history restores that setting and follows its subsequent reputation.

This edition presents the complete story in its original British text. The textual history and note on the apparatus distinguish Blackwood’s narrative from modern explanations added around it. There are no footnotes in the story itself; the notes at the end of each section give facts and do not interpret the supernatural events.

sections.heading: The journey behind the fiction
paragraphs: Blackwood made a real canoe journey on the Danube. The edition examines the accounts of that trip, including his own recollections, and records the uncertainty about its date. Accounts give 1900 or 1901, and the edition reports the disagreement.

The documentary material provides information about travel, camping and the river route that can be compared with the story. The real journey and the story are treated separately. A resemblance between a remembered landscape and a description establishes a useful context, but does not establish that the narrator’s whole experience happened to the author.

sections.heading: A river landscape that has changed
paragraphs: The names and places in the narrative belong to the historical Danube. Pressburg is the city now called Bratislava, and the channels below it form the geographical setting for the canoeists’ difficulty. The edition supplies historical geography so that readers can locate this stretch of river without expecting present-day maps to reproduce the landscape as described.

Material on later river engineering explains why that comparison has limits. Major works and the diversion of water into the Gabčíkovo power canal in 1992 substantially altered the area. These changes are discussed as part of the site’s history, not as evidence for the story’s supernatural claims. The geographical account also explains the practical significance of flooding, unstable banks and changing channels.

sections.heading: Blackwood and the history of the weird tale
paragraphs: Algernon Blackwood lived from 1869 to 1951. His career included fiction, journalism and later radio and television appearances. The biographical material places the story within his travelling and writing life and considers the supernatural and occult interests that form part of its historical background.

The reception account treats H. P. Lovecraft’s praise with attention to the actual wording of Supernatural Horror in Literature. The sentence often quoted as calling The Willows the finest supernatural tale in English literature paraphrases his high opinion; it is not a quotation. The edition explains that distinction and places his response alongside the broader history of the story’s circulation.

sections.heading: What the notes are for
paragraphs: Section summaries help a reader keep track of the two men’s observations, their changing assessment of their situation and their attempts to manage the camp. The factual notes explain geography, canoe travel, unfamiliar language and documented background. They are designed for reference while leaving the story’s account of its events available to the reader.

The longer material brings together the author’s life, the evidence for the real voyage, publication history and the changing physical landscape. It is particularly useful when a modern retelling has encouraged assumptions about the story’s setting or when a familiar statement about its reputation proves to be a paraphrase. The volume identifies what is documented and where the record remains uncertain, alongside the complete work of fiction.

title: Three Men in a Boat
image: Three Men in a Boat Main Cover.png
author: Jerome K. Jerome
summary: J., George and Harris decide that what they need is a rest, and take a boat up the Thames from Kingston to Oxford with a fox terrier called Montmorency. Jerome K. Jerome meant the book to be a guide to the river with jokes in it; the jokes took over. This edition reproduces A. Frederics’s illustrations of 1889.
editionIncludes: Complete 1889 text, preserving original spelling and punctuation
Original illustrations by A. Frederics, reproduced from the 1889 first edition
Chapter summaries and researched historical context
Original material on the Victorian Thames, boats, camping, prices and customs
Publication, illustration and reception histories and the real people behind the travellers

sections.heading: The journey and its interruptions
paragraphs: J., George and Harris decide that a holiday on the river will improve their health. They take Montmorency, a fox terrier, and set out on the Thames with the intention of combining exercise and rest. Packing, finding food, managing a tow-line and arranging a night’s shelter repeatedly become more difficult than their confident preparations suggest.

The book follows the river journey, with many stops for remembered incidents, arguments, stories about friends and facts about the places they pass. The result is not simply a day-by-day travel log. Jerome’s narrator moves between the present trip and anecdotes prompted by what the men see or attempt to do.

sections.heading: The original publication
paragraphs: Three Men in a Boat was serialised in Home Chimes before its publication by J. W. Arrowsmith in 1889. The Jerome K. Jerome Society’s formal bibliography records the serial from September–December 1888 and January–June 1889. Arrowsmith’s own later advertisement dates the first book publication to August 1889.

The original subtitle is To Say Nothing of the Dog. This Astor edition preserves the complete 1889 text, including its spelling and punctuation, and reproduces the original illustrations by A. Frederics. Their presence is an edition feature: the drawings themselves accompany the text, in addition to the separate discussion of their publication history.

sections.heading: J., George, Harris and Montmorency
paragraphs: The travellers draw on Jerome and two friends, George Wingrave and Carl Hentschel. The supporting account identifies these men while explaining the changes made in the fiction. Hentschel, associated with Harris, was a teetotaller despite the drinking attributed to the fictional character. A biographical model therefore does not make every episode a factual record of that person’s conduct.

Montmorency was invented. Jerome’s later account of the dog is treated separately from the lives of the three men, and the distinction is preserved in the edition’s discussion. This information is useful when the easy familiarity of the narration makes the whole journey appear to be straightforward autobiography.

sections.heading: The Victorian Thames
paragraphs: The historical sections follow the places and practices that occur in the narrative: locks, towing, camping, meals, boats and the cost of a river holiday. These details explain what the travellers are trying to do before the comedy develops from their failures. They also make it possible to distinguish a historical practice from something a modern reader might assume about recreational boating.

The edition supplies factual material on prices, laws and customs associated with the journey. Jerome’s digressions into local history are considered alongside the places that prompt them. Readers can follow the route as a journey through an inhabited and managed river landscape, including its towns, landing places and other river users.

sections.heading: Illustration, printing and reception
paragraphs: A. Frederics’s pictures were printed in the text, not as separate plates. Their reproduction here preserves a feature of the 1889 book that is easily lost in editions presenting only the prose. The illustration history explains their place in the original publication without implying that modern copies are printed from the original physical blocks.

The reception history treats figures and recollections with care. Arrowsmith’s 1909 advertisement records 202,000 copies produced during the book’s first twenty years; that is a production figure, not an independently established sales total. Likewise, famous hostile review quotations known from Jerome’s later memoir are identified as his retrospective testimony when their original newspaper issue, date and page have not been established.

sections.heading: Reading with the Astor material
paragraphs: Chapter-end summaries and Context material provide the annotation. No new editorial footnotes have been inserted into the narrative. A reader can check the progress of the journey, consult the historical background to an episode and then return to Jerome’s text and Frederics’s drawings.

The supporting material also covers Jerome’s career, publication, illustration and reception, and the circumstances behind the familiar characters. Its reference points are the actual river, the nineteenth-century book and the documentary record of its circulation. Together with the complete illustrated text, those sections support reading Three Men in a Boat both as a comic narrative and as a book made for the late-Victorian reading public.

title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
author: Mark Twain
summary: Tom Sawyer tricks the boys of St. Petersburg, Missouri, into whitewashing his aunt’s fence for him, runs off to be a pirate on Jackson’s Island, and with Huck Finn sees a murder in the graveyard at midnight. Twain drew the town from Hannibal, where he grew up in the 1840s. The book appeared in 1876, in London before New York.
editionIncludes: Complete novel, preserving Twain’s text
Chapter summaries and historical context
Publication and textual history, including the British, Canadian and American editions
Original essays on Hannibal, slavery, childhood, schooling and superstition
Contemporary reception and discussion of the original illustration programme

sections.heading: Tom’s life in St Petersburg
paragraphs: Tom Sawyer lives with Aunt Polly in St Petersburg, a fictional Missouri town on the Mississippi. His efforts to evade work and school include the whitewashing scheme, while his friendships and rivalries involve Huckleberry Finn, Joe Harper and Becky Thatcher. Play, punishment and the attraction of independence are recurring parts of his life in the town.

The adventures acquire a different urgency when Tom and Huck witness a murder in the graveyard. Tom must decide what to do with knowledge that puts another man at risk and threatens his own safety. The later search for treasure and the cave episode connect the boys’ imagined adventures with events that have consequences beyond a game.

sections.heading: The unusual route into print
paragraphs: The first edition appeared in London through Chatto & Windus on 9 June 1876, ahead of the authorised American edition. Belford Brothers issued an unauthorised Canadian edition in Toronto on 29 July. The American Publishing Company’s edition followed in December 1876. The publication history records all three first appearances: London, then Toronto, and only then the United States.

The delay allowed Canadian copies and widely reprinted newspaper extracts to reach readers before the authorised American book was available. Twain’s suspicions about stolen proofs are distinguished from what can be established about the piracy. The edition explains these events as part of the work’s publishing history and its disappointing initial commercial performance.

sections.heading: The text and the early illustrations
paragraphs: The Astor volume preserves the complete novel while adding chapter summaries, historical context and material on textual and publication history. The story is printed in full, from the early scenes at home through the murder and the cave to the arrangements made for Tom and Huck at the end.

True W. Williams supplied the great majority of the original American illustrations, with some work by others. Those pictures and their role in marketing the book are discussed in the editorial material, but they are not reproduced in this edition. This distinction matters for readers choosing a copy: illustration history is part of the commentary, while the printed reading text is accompanied by modern contextual material.

sections.heading: Hannibal and the historical town
paragraphs: St Petersburg draws on Hannibal, where Samuel Langhorne Clemens grew up before adopting the name Mark Twain. The Mississippi, the nearby cave, local schooling, churches and the social life of the town provide identifiable contexts for the fiction. The edition gives factual information about those settings while distinguishing them from the novel’s rearrangement of people and events.

Slavery is part of that history and of the world represented in the book. The historical sections do not describe the town only through the freedom available to Tom and his friends. They also attend to the people whose work and legal position made that childhood society possible, placing the novel’s incidents beside the record of Missouri life before the Civil War.

sections.heading: Childhood, language and belief
paragraphs: Schoolroom exchanges, Sunday-school prizes, punishments, courtship rituals and the boys’ plans for piracy make up much of the book’s social detail. The accompanying material explains the customs and institutions behind these episodes. It also considers the superstitions associated with the graveyard visit and the methods the boys propose for solving practical problems.

Twain’s language is printed as he wrote it. Contextual material helps identify historical vocabulary, social assumptions and the difference between the narrator’s account and the boys’ explanations. The edition follows the events closely enough for readers to see when a game, a belief or a private promise becomes relevant to a later decision.

sections.heading: Twain’s reputation and later accounts
paragraphs: The reception material examines contemporary responses and the book’s subsequent standing, together with the circumstances of its first sales. It also checks later anecdotes. Twain’s recollection that Tom Sawyer was his typewritten literary manuscript is treated as an unreliable memory; the discussion identifies Life on the Mississippi as the more likely work involved.

The volume brings these histories together with the complete novel: the real Hannibal, the fictional St Petersburg, the British first edition, Canadian piracy and the American illustrated book. Chapter summaries and critical background provide ways to study the narrative, while the publication record shows how the form and availability of the book differed for its first readers.

author: William Shakespeare
summary: Shakespeare’s two complete narrative poems, based on the quartos of 1593 and 1594, with modernised spelling and punctuation, line numbers and same-page explanatory notes. Introductions, contextual essays, close readings and a glossary accompany the poems.
editionIncludes: Complete texts of Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece

Modernised spelling and punctuation, preserving wording, stanza forms and rhyme
Line numbers and explanatory notes printed on the same page as the poetry
Introductions, classical sources, critical approaches, close readings and glossary

sections.heading: Two early books by Shakespeare
paragraphs: Venus and Adonis was published in 1593 and Lucrece in 1594. Both were dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, Earl of Southampton. These dates belong to the works’ first appearance as printed books, and the dedications are important contemporary evidence of how Shakespeare presented his poetry to a patron and to readers.

Venus and Adonis was repeatedly reprinted during Shakespeare’s lifetime. Lucrece followed as a more extended treatment of a Roman story. The Astor volume brings both poems together complete, enabling readers to compare their narratives and verse forms while retaining the historical distinction between their original publications.

sections.heading: Venus and Adonis
paragraphs: Venus pursues the young hunter Adonis, who resists her advances and wishes to return to hunting. Much of the poem consists of her attempts to persuade him and of his replies. The narrative also includes the episode of his horse and a mare, before following the consequences of Adonis’s fatal encounter with a boar.

The poem develops material from the story of Venus and Adonis in Ovid’s Metamorphoses. Shakespeare expands the exchange between the two figures into a sustained verbal and physical encounter. The notes explain classical references, unfamiliar words and rhetorical devices, so readers can follow the argument from stanza to stanza.

sections.heading: Lucrece and the Roman narrative
paragraphs: The Rape of Lucrece concerns Tarquin’s assault on Lucrece, the wife of Collatine, and its aftermath. Tarquin’s deliberations and Lucrece’s speech occupy a much larger part of the poem than a short account of the incident would suggest. After the assault she seeks to report what has happened to her husband and others.

The story belongs to Roman accounts of the expulsion of the kings and the establishment of the republic. Shakespeare’s poem includes Lucrece’s extended response to a picture of the fall of Troy before returning to her testimony and death. The supporting material explains the classical setting and the narrative’s movement from an individual crime to public action.

sections.heading: Verse, language and the edited text
paragraphs: The reading text is based on the quartos of 1593 and 1594. Spelling and punctuation are modernised, while Shakespeare’s wording, stanza forms and rhyme are preserved. This is a modernised reading edition: its presentation makes an explicit distinction between alterations to spelling and punctuation and changes to the substance of the poems.

Venus and Adonis uses six-line stanzas, while Lucrece uses seven-line rhyme-royal stanzas. The printed line numbers and same-page notes provide a way to follow references and return to particular passages. Explanations address difficult vocabulary, allusions and figures of speech in relation to the lines where they occur.

sections.heading: Sources, contexts and close reading
paragraphs: The introductions and essays cover classical sources, publication, language, style and the main figures in each narrative. Close readings follow particular exchanges and passages, including persuasion and refusal in Venus and Adonis and Lucrece’s attempts to describe the wrong done to her. They give readers evidence to work with.

Reading the two works in one volume also permits comparisons between their different speakers and outcomes. Venus’s direct appeals, Adonis’s resistance, Tarquin’s self-argument and Lucrece’s addresses to personified forces are distinct uses of speech. The commentary helps identify those formal differences while keeping the complete passages available for judgement.

sections.heading: Reference material and study
paragraphs: A glossary supplies a further route into recurring language, alongside the notes attached to individual lines. Material on reception, critical approaches and teaching gives additional points of entry for readers studying the poems after an initial reading. The supporting essays remain separate from the texts, so that the poems can be read continuously or consulted passage by passage.

The combined edition is particularly useful for work on Shakespeare’s early publication, his handling of classical stories and the relationship between narrative and argument in verse. Both poems are printed complete. The original dates, the quarto basis, the modernisation policy and the location of the explanatory notes are stated so readers can identify the kind of text and assistance the volume provides.

title: Victorian Ghost Stories
author: Elizabeth Gaskell, Charles Dickens and others
deck: Eight Victorian ghost stories and four poems, from Gaskell to Stoker.
editorial: Stories, poems and documents, 1844–1901, with notes.

sections.heading: The writers represented
paragraphs: The prose selection brings together Elizabeth Gaskell, Edward Bulwer-Lytton, Mary Elizabeth Braddon, Amelia B. Edwards, Charles Dickens, Margaret Oliphant, E. Nesbit and Bram Stoker. Most of them also wrote novels and journalism; they were not a school, and each ghost story was written for a particular magazine or Christmas number.

The collection’s literary contributors also include Thomas Hood, Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Christina Rossetti. Its four complete poems give verse a separate place within the volume. The subtitle’s date range, 1844–1901, applies to the anthology of stories, poems and documents as a whole. It should not be read as a publication date for every story, or as a claim that the eight prose texts alone cover all those years.

sections.heading: Christmas issues and the periodical record
paragraphs: Gaskell’s ‘The Old Nurse’s Story’ appeared in the 1852 Christmas number of Household Words. The journal’s surviving office records, indexed by Dickens Journals Online, identify Gaskell as its author and record a payment of £10. Records like these tie the story to a particular commission and issue.

Dickens’s ‘The Signal-Man’ appeared in the 1866 Christmas number of All the Year Round, Mugby Junction, under the heading ‘No. 1 Branch Line’. The railway setting therefore belonged to the organising subject of the issue as well as to the individual tale. Reading the stories in a later anthology changes their immediate surroundings: notes on first publication restore information about the magazines and collective projects in which readers originally encountered them.

sections.heading: Literary ghosts and organised inquiry
paragraphs: The documentary material places literary apparitions beside historical discussion of spiritualism and psychical research. The Society for Psychical Research was founded in London in February 1882 after a January conference considering how such claims might be investigated. Its first president was the Cambridge philosopher Henry Sidgwick; early associates included Frederic Myers and Edmund Gurney.

The society developed journals, records of testimony and investigative procedures. Its work included examining apparent manifestations for possible deception as well as collecting accounts of unusual experiences. These activities provide a context for the anthology’s documents, but a report of an apparition and a fictional ghost story have different purposes and evidential status. The collection’s separate literary and documentary sections allow those differences to remain visible while readers compare vocabulary, settings, witnesses and the methods used to describe or question supernatural events.
Organised psychical inquiry thus developed during the period covered by the anthology, decades after its earliest literary material had first appeared.

title: White Fang
author: Jack London
summary: White Fang, three-quarters wolf, is born in the Yukon wild and passes from a Native owner, Gray Beaver, to a dog-fighter called Beauty Smith before a mining engineer, Weedon Scott, takes him home to California. Jack London wrote it in 1906 as a companion to The Call of the Wild, with the journey running the other way.
editionIncludes: Complete 1906 text with notes on the Macmillan edition
Chapter summaries and historical context at chapter ends
Original essays on the Klondike, sled-dog culture and animal fiction
Critical perspectives, characters and reception history
Publication history and discussion of the nature-faker controversy

sections.heading: From the Northland to California
paragraphs: White Fang follows a wolfdog born in the Northland whose life changes as he encounters different human owners. His early experience involves hunger and competition before he comes into the household of Grey Beaver. Work, punishment and conflict with other dogs shape what he learns about people and how to survive among them.

Beauty Smith subsequently uses him for fighting, and Weedon Scott rescues him from that life. The later part of the novel follows White Fang to California, where the conditions of a settled household require different behaviour. White Fang’s nature changes with each owner.

sections.heading: The 1906 publication
paragraphs: White Fang first appeared in six monthly instalments in Outing from May to October 1906. Macmillan published the book in October of the same year. The Astor publication history records both the serial and the book, distinguishing the work’s first circulation from the form in which readers later commonly encountered it.

The original Macmillan edition contained a colour frontispiece and seven further colour plates by Charles Livingston Bull. Its publishing history also involves differences between surviving title leaves, whose priority has been disputed. The edition discusses these bibliographical matters without presenting an uncertain first-state sequence as an established fact.

sections.heading: The text and editorial apparatus
paragraphs: This edition preserves London’s 1906 text and supplies textual notes on the Macmillan version. The story itself has no footnotes, and none have been introduced. Chapter-end summaries and historical context carry the annotation, while the longer original material appears in the surrounding editorial sections.

The arrangement allows the animal narrative to be read continuously, with summaries available for reviewing the sequence of events. Contextual essays then provide information about places, work, travel, influences and publication. The critical and reception sections are kept separate from London’s text.

sections.heading: London and the Klondike
paragraphs: Jack London lived from 1876 to 1916. His writing career included novels, stories, journalism and nonfiction, and his journey to the Klondike supplied experience later used in a range of works. The edition places White Fang within that career and gives historical context for the gold rush and the movement of people into the Yukon.

The supporting sections examine sled-dog culture, transport, labour and the practical demands of northern travel. They distinguish these historical circumstances from the novel’s particular scenes. Food, ownership, trade and the treatment of working dogs are all part of the world White Fang enters.

sections.heading: Animal fiction and the nature-faker dispute
paragraphs: The novel was published three years after The Call of the Wild. The two works follow contrasting movements: Buck is taken from domestic life into the North and eventually joins the wild, while White Fang’s history moves towards a human household. Reading the books together makes that difference in their narratives immediately visible.

The edition also discusses the nature-faker controversy, in which writers disputed the accuracy of representations of animal behaviour. Theodore Roosevelt criticised the fighting episode involving the bulldog Cherokee. London’s response, The Other Animals, appeared in Collier’s on 5 September 1908. These records give a specific historical basis for considering what London claimed about animal reasoning and what his critics challenged.

sections.heading: Reception and reading the whole novel
paragraphs: Publication and reception sections trace the book’s subsequent circulation and its adaptations. They keep the original novel distinct from later screen versions. The bibliographical account also distinguishes a reprinting from an original printing: by August 1912, the Macmillan publication record lists five reprintings after the October 1906 issue.

The complete text is accompanied by character material, critical perspectives and researched chapter-end context. Readers can follow the successive conditions of White Fang’s life and then consult information about the Klondike, dog teams, London’s writing and debates about animal fiction. The textual note identifies the source of the reading text, while the historical and critical sections give readers separate ways to investigate its publication, setting and reception.
